# THE BOOK ON THE COMPOSITION OF ALCHEMY,
## which Morienus the Roman <note>Morienus is a legendary figure in alchemical lore, often depicted as a hermit living near Jerusalem who taught the secrets of the Philosopher's Stone to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> produced for Khalid, King of the Egyptians: Which Robert of Chester <note>Robert of Chester (Robertus Castrensis) was an English scholar of the 12th century who was among the first to translate Arabic mathematical and alchemical works into Latin, effectively introducing these sciences to Western Europe.</note> translated from Arabic into Latin.

## PREFACE BY ROBERT OF CHESTER.

<image-desc>Ornate decorative woodcut initial 'L' depicting a figure (likely a scholar or philosopher) in a classical landscape with buildings and foliage in the background.</image-desc>*WE READ in the histories of the ancient divines that there were three Philosophers, each of whom was called Hermes. The first of them was Enoch <note>The author identifies the biblical patriarch Enoch with Hermes; Enoch was frequently associated with hidden knowledge and the invention of writing.</note>, who by another name was called Hermes, and by another name Mercurius. The second was Noah, who similarly by another name was called Hermes, and by another name Mercurius. The third of them was Hermes, who reigned in Egypt after the flood, and held his kingdom for a long time. This man was called “Triple” <note>original: "Triplex." This refers to Hermes Trismegistus, or "Hermes the Thrice-Greatest."</note> by our ancestors, because of his threefold* <note>The text likely continues to explain the "threefold" nature of his wisdom—traditionally king, philosopher, and prophet, or his mastery of the three parts of the wisdom of the whole world.</note>

<summary>This page introduces the "Book on the Composition of Alchemy," beginning with a preface by the translator Robert of Chester that traces the lineage of the legendary Hermes Trismegistus through biblical figures like Enoch and Noah.</summary>
<keywords>Morienus Romanus, Khalid ibn Yazid, Robert of Chester, Hermes Trismegistus, Enoch, Noah, alchemy, history of science, Egyptian kings</keywords>

# PREFACE.

*...a collection of virtues, clearly attributed to him by the Lord God. Moreover, he was a King, a philosopher, and a prophet. This was truly that Hermes, who after the Flood <note>original: "diluvium"; referring to the biblical flood of Noah, a common chronological marker in medieval histories.</note> was the first inventor and author of all arts and disciplines, both liberal <note>The "liberal arts" (artes liberales) were the seven subjects of classical education: grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy.</note> and mechanical <note>The "mechanical arts" (artes mechanicae) referred to practical crafts and applied sciences, such as metalworking, medicine, and agriculture.</note>. For all those who came after him strove to walk in his path and to follow in his footsteps. Why say more? It would be a long task for us, and even a difficult one, to bring back to memory at present the ornaments of virtue and the deeds of so great and eminent a man. Since we have not undertaken this kind of teaching in the translation of this divine book; nor indeed could the thinness of our intellect, or our study, or the labor of writing, suffice to explain this to you. But we have introduced his name into the Prologue of this book for this reason: because he was the first to find and publish this book. For this is a divine book, and most full of divinity. In it is contained the true and perfect proof of the two testaments (namely, the Old and the New). For if anyone studies much in this book, and understands it fully—*

<summary>Robert of Chester identifies Hermes Trismegistus as the post-Flood inventor of all sciences and the original author of this alchemical work, which he claims provides proof for both the Old and New Testaments.</summary>
<keywords>Hermes Trismegistus, liberal arts, mechanical arts, Robert of Chester, alchemy and scripture, history of science, post-diluvian knowledge</keywords>

# PREFACE.

...clearly understood, the truth and virtue of the testament, as well as the way of both lives <note>This likely refers to the active and contemplative lives, or perhaps the physical and spiritual lives, common themes in medieval theology.</note>, will not be able to remain hidden from him. This, then, is the book which is named the *Book on the Composition of Alchemy*. And since your Latin world <note>original: "latinitas"; Robert is addressing the scholars of Western Europe who read and wrote in Latin, to whom the Arabic science of alchemy was still largely unknown in the 12th century.</note> does not yet truly know what Alchemy is, nor what its composition might be, I shall clarify it in the present discourse. I have put forward this word, although it is unknown and strange, so that it might become clear through a definition.

Indeed, Hermes the philosopher, and others who followed after him, define this term in the *Book on the Change of Substances* as follows: "Alchemy is a corporeal substance composed of one and through one, joining together more precious things to one another by kinship and effect, and by the same natural mixing, transforming them naturally into better natures." <note>This definition presents alchemy as a natural science of transformation, suggesting that all things come from a single source ("the one") and can be improved through their inherent relationships.</note>

In what follows, what we have said will be explained; and there, its composition will be treated fully. But we, although our intellect is still young and our Latinity very modest, have nevertheless undertaken to translate this great and significant work from Arabic into Latin. From which also...

# PREFACE.

*For the singular grace bestowed upon us by God among men of our time <note>original: "modernos"; Robert is referring to his contemporaries in the 12th century, a period of massive intellectual transition as Arabic science entered Europe.</note>, we give thanks to that highest living God, who exists as three and one <note>A reference to the Christian Trinity, framing the study of alchemy within a religious worldview.</note>. It did not please me, however, to keep my name hidden at the beginning of the Prologue, lest someone else should take this labor of ours for himself, and also claim its praise and merit as if it were his own. What more? I humbly ask and beseech everyone that none of our people waste away with envy <note>original: "livore"; literally "lividness" or "bruising," a term frequently used in the Middle Ages to describe the spiritual sickness of jealousy toward another's success.</note> toward my name (as many are often known to do). For the God of all knows upon whom He bestows His grace; and the Spirit proceeds from grace, who inspires whom He wills. Rightly, therefore, we ought to rejoice, when the creator and founder of all things shows to all people*

->*His divinity,*<-
->*as it were,*<-
->*particularly.*<-

<summary>Robert of Chester concludes his preface by identifying himself as the translator to protect his intellectual labor from plagiarism. He frames the introduction of alchemy to the West as a divine gift and asks his readers to receive it with gratitude rather than jealousy.</summary>

# MORIENUS THE ROMAN,
## HERMIT OF JERU-
### salem, a Discourse.

<image-desc>A square decorative woodcut initial 'O' featuring a central flower surrounded by symmetrical acanthus-style leaves and floral flourishes, set within a double-line border.</image-desc>

The divine mind of Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary "Thrice-Great" founder of alchemy, often conflated with the Egyptian god Thoth.</note> fully grasped all parts of philosophy. After he had studied for many years in the discovery and publication of the superior mastery <note>original: "magisterium"; in alchemy, the "magistery" refers to the entire process of creating the Philosopher's Stone or the perfected work itself.</note>, he was the first to find and set it forth. He composed a book about it, which he claimed as his own work, and after his death, he left it to his disciples as an inheritance. After his death, however, his disciples studied this book and its precepts for a long time, so that they might be able to achieve its intended result. 

After they had finally obtained that result, they gave various and even innumerable instructions concerning it. They did this so that those who attained this knowledge after them would not reveal it as if it were something common <note>original: "vulgarem"; the authors suggest that "common" or "vulgar" people lack the spiritual discipline to handle such power.</note> to the foolish. A long time after the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, there arose a certain divine man, endowed with spiritual gifts, who, having studied divinity for a great deal of time, found this book among the sacred writings. Now this man was a native of Alexandria; hence, he was called by his name, Adfar the Alexandrian <note>Adfar (often identified with Stephanus of Alexandria) is portrayed here as the person who rediscovered the lost Hermetic secrets, eventually passing them to Morienus.</note>. This man, after he...

<summary>This page introduces the history of the alchemical "magistery," tracing it from its origin with the divine Hermes to its rediscovery by Adfar of Alexandria. It emphasizes that the art was intentionally obscured by early disciples to prevent the "foolish" from accessing its secrets.</summary>

...found the aforementioned book <note>The word fragment "brum" completes "librum" (book) from the previous page.</note>, he did not cease to study it with a watchful mind and great industry. After he had indeed studied it for a long time, he achieved its effect and knowledge to the fullest. From this knowledge, therefore, this divine man gave many varied and innumerable instructions; when these had been spread under his name through all parts of our region, the fame of this man's name and of that science reached me as if on wings, while I was staying at that time in the city of Rome. For at that time I was situated in Rome (where I was also born).

I was then a youth, whose chin the first down had not yet covered, being a student and having been made a Christian in doctrine from the earliest stage of my life by both of my parents; to me, all Latinity <note>original: "latinitas"; this refers to the complete mastery of Latin grammar, rhetoric, and the classical literary tradition.</note> had already revealed itself. Therefore, having heard this man's name and fame, I hastily abandoned my parents and my homeland alike, nor did I yield my limbs to excessive rest until I had arrived at Alexandria.

I entered the city, and walked through the streets and alleys as a new guest for a long time, until I had found this man’s house. At last, I found his home and entered it; having entered, I found this man sitting in his oratory <note>original: "oratorium"; a private room dedicated to prayer, reflection, and study.</note> and studying his books. But after he fixed his eyes upon me, looking at me, he said: "Friend, come here." I then approached him, and stood beside him...

<header>ON THE TRANSMUTATION OF METALS 9</header>

I sat down upon the matting <note>original: "stramentum"; this refers to straw or a simple woven mat used for seating.</note> that had been placed there. He was a man already very advanced in age, but still vigorous in his expression, and handsome in both his face and his physical stature. Indeed, his countenance revealed to those who looked closely all the thoughts that lay hidden in his mind. After we had conversed for a while, he asked what my name was, where I had been born, and what the purpose of my journey had been. I answered him, saying: "I am called Morienus, a Roman by birth; it was the fame of your name and knowledge that compelled me to leave my parents and my homeland." To this he added: "What is your faith, and which of the gods do you worship?" I replied: "I profess the Christian faith, for I am a follower of Christ, and I adore Him as the triune and one God <note>A reference to the Christian doctrine of the Trinity.</note>." 

Then Adfar said: "It is well that you have sought me out, and that you have found me while I am still enclosed in this worldly frame <note>original: "homine mundano septum"; this likely refers to being still alive in his physical, earthly body before death.</note>. For I shall reveal to you the secrets of all divinity, which until now I have refused to disclose to almost anyone. But you must attend to me with all the strength of your mind; for I will make you a son of all my teachings <note>original: "disciplinae filium"; in alchemical tradition, an apprentice was often called a 'son of the art' or 'son of the doctrine,' implying a spiritual lineage rather than a biological one.</note>." 

When these things had been said by both of us, I rejoiced with exceeding joy. What more can I say? It would be a long task to list and describe every detail of what we discussed regarding the instructions of this work. I remained with him at last, and made myself so dear to him...

<header>MORIENUS THE ROMAN</header>

...I had shown, because he had told me the secrets of all divinity. Afterward, Adfar died. A few days after his passing, I departed from Alexandria and came to Jerusalem. In that region, I chose a hermitage <term>eremus; a secluded place for spiritual retreat, often a desert cell or cave</term> for myself, where I might lead a life suited to my faith and my calling.

Not many years later, a certain king named Macoya <note>original: "Macoya"; likely referring to Mu’awiya I (r. 661–680 AD), the founder of the Umayyad Caliphate.</note> rose to power in Egypt. He fathered a son named Gezid <note>original: "Gezid"; referring to Yazid I.</note>, who ruled in Egypt after his father's death and held his kingdom. Gezid then fathered a son named Calid <note>original: "Calid"; referring to Khalid ibn Yazid, an Umayyad prince who, according to legend, was the first Muslim to study alchemy.</note>, who reigned for a long time in Egypt after his father’s death.

This King was a wise and discerning man, clear-sighted in every branch of knowledge. He had a great love for the wise and for philosophers because of the knowledge contained in this book <note>original: "huius libri scientiam"; here "this book" refers to the secret art of alchemy, which the text treats as a singular, divine body of knowledge.</note>. He did not stop searching throughout the provinces, questioning both the famous and the unknown, to see if he could find anyone who could reveal the teachings of this book to him. 

Driven by this passion, he kept many so-called wise men and philosophers at his side who claimed to possess the mastery of this book, even though they were entirely ignorant of it. He enriched these men with many grand gifts, having trusted their words for a long time. 

One day, while I was in my hermitage, the fame of this king was brought to me by a traveler. When I heard of him, I left my retreat and, as quickly as I could, <meta>catchword: toward his (ad suae)</meta>

# ON THE TRANSMUTATION OF METALS

I traveled to the borders of his region; not indeed to seek riches or gifts from him, but so that I might diligently instruct him in spiritual gifts. Truly, after I entered his territory, I surveyed many places as I went, and at last, I found the king. When I had found him and conferred with him on certain matters, I found him to be a man of great wisdom, adorned with every virtue, and most prudent. Therefore I said to him: "O good king, may God turn you toward the better <note>original: "Deus te ad melius conuertat"; a traditional blessing wishing for the King's spiritual enlightenment.</note>. I desire, however, that you order a house to be prepared for me, one suitable for my mastery <term>magisterium; the "mastery" refers to the successful completion of the Great Work of alchemy</term>."

...to the judgment of this **mastery** <term>magisterium|The secret art of alchemy or the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</term>, and you shall know it well and understand it. But remember to study its beginning and its end <note>original: "introitu & exitu"; referring to the initial entrance into the work and its final completion</note> deeply; because, with the Lord's favor, you will more easily attain everything that pertains to it.

For this thing, which you have sought for so long, is not obtained or accomplished through force or anger. Rather, it is received through patience, humility, and a certain and most perfect love. When this knowledge has been granted to any of His faithful, it is fitting for him to first look ahead to see whom he might later entrust with it and to whom he might reveal it. For this thing can be nothing other than a **gift of the Most High God** <term>donum Dei|A central alchemical tenet: that the ultimate secret cannot be learned by effort alone, but must be granted by God to the virtuous</term>, who entrusts and shows it to whichever of His servants and faithful He wishes. **O**mnipotent <note>original: "Omnipotens"</note> Lord and Creator of all things, out of His almighty power, created the healthy and powerful: for they themselves are unable to change their order. For this is the knowledge that draws its master away from the misery of this world and leads him back to the knowledge of future blessings. In times past, they always inherited this **wisdom** <term>sapientia|Often used interchangeably with the 'Art' or the 'Stone' itself</term> from one another in turn; but afterward, this knowledge was almost held in contempt. That which most effectively joins these bodies together is the **blood** <term>Sanguis|In alchemical texts, "blood" rarely refers to the biological fluid; it typically signifies a vitalizing mineral spirit, a red-colored solvent, or a "soul" that binds the solid "body" and volatile "spirit" together.</term>. For this reason, a gentle fire must be applied for a longer time, which should always remain equal throughout its days. For if the heat of the fire creeps too quickly into the body, it consumes that body with a hasty combustion.

For once bodies no longer retain their **souls** <note>original: "animas"; referring to the volatile elements that give the metal its characteristic properties.</note>, they are quickly burned. Eudica (the dross of glass) indeed suits all bodies well: for it vivifies and prepares them, and defends them from all burning. It introduces certain elements of them into others, and after they are introduced, it protects them together from excessive heat.

And when you wish to seek eudica, look for it in glass vessels: when you have found it, store it away, and do nothing with it until it becomes acidic. Let it not be **unleavened** <note>original: "azima"; a term borrowed from bread-making, suggesting the substance must "ferment" or be activated by an acidic catalyst rather than remaining "flat" or inert.</note>, for then your intention would be utterly destroyed.

### *Wise, for the adaptation of the unclean body <note>original: "corpus immundi"; refers to the base metal or raw material before it has been purified through alchemical processes.</note>, before the* Elixir *is placed upon that body (which has been made clean and hard), and before it is made white, and before the soul <note>original: "anima"; in alchemy, the 'soul' often refers to the volatile spirit or the "tincture" that gives the metal its new properties.</note> is sent into it.*

Begin, therefore, under God’s help, and first make it so that the red smoke <note>original: "fumus rubeus"; alchemical vapors, often associated with sulfurous or solar principles.</note> takes the white smoke <note>original: "fumus albus"; vapors associated with mercurial or lunar principles.</note>, and pour them both down and join them together, in such a way that in their mixing an equal weight of each is applied. ## HERE BEGINS THE EXPLANATION
### *of the materials.*

Morienus said: O good and most wise king, this is the explanation of the materials which pertain to this mastery, which our predecessors named with many and diverse names so that those who sought this mastery unworthily would wander completely away from its truth. Know therefore, that the **unclean body** is lead, which is interpreted by another name as *Affrop* <note>original: "Affrop", likely a Latinized version of the Arabic 'al-usrub', meaning lead.</note>. The **clean body**, however, is tin, which is also called by the name *Arena* <note>literally "sand".</note>. The **green lion** <term>leo viridis|A common alchemical metaphor. While often meaning vitriol or antimony, here Morienus specifically identifies it with glass or the material used to make it.</term> is glass; *Almagra* <note>usually referring to red ochre or red earth.</note> is also **brass** <term>laton|A brass-like alloy of copper and zinc.</term>, although we said above that it was red earth. Blood is also **orpiment** <term>auripigmentum|Arsenic trisulfide, a yellow mineral used as a pigment and in alchemy.</term>, and the **stinking earth** is stinking sulfur.

But also **Eudica** <term>Eudica|Mentioned on the previous page as a stabilizing additive; here defined as the "feces" or dregs of glass-making.</term> is the secret of all these things, which is called by another name *Moszhacumia*, which in Latin can be called the "dross of glass" or the "impurity of glass." **Red smoke** is red orpiment <note>likely realgar, an arsenic sulfide mineral.</note>; **white smoke** is **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum|Mercury.</term>; and **yellow smoke** is yellow sulfur. Behold, I now declare to you the names of the materials, of which three alone will suffice for you for the whole mastery: that is, **white smoke**, the **green lion**, and **stinking water**. Likewise, you should know that the greater root of this work lies in the investigation of the species <term>species|In this context, the specific types of minerals or raw materials used as the starting point for the work.</term> which are better for this mastery <term>magisterium|The "Mastery" or Great Work; the complete process of alchemical transformation.</term>. A symbolic term for the volatile spirit or vapor that rises during distillation, often associated with the 'Albedo' or whitening stage.</note> about which you asked, it is fitting for you to know that the **white smoke** is the **tincture** <term>tinctura|The transforming essence or "dye" that changes the color and nature of a base metal into a noble one.</term>, and it is also the **soul** of these dissolved and even "dead" bodies. These are the souls, you see, which we have already extracted and then joined once again to their bodies. 

For every body, when it lacks a soul, will be dark and obscure; and the **white smoke** is that which flows into the body, just like a soul, so that it may completely remove its **blackness** <note>original: "nigredinem". Referring to the *Nigredo* stage of decay and darkness.</note> and its impurity from it. It consolidates the bodies into one and multiplies their "water." For that which is impure is black and very light; and therefore when its blackness is taken away, its **whiteness** <note>original: "albedo". The second major stage of the work, representing purification and brilliance.</note> is strengthened, its water is multiplied, and its beauty will be more apparent. The tincture will then work more effectively within it. 

What more can be said? If all these things are handled well, the tincture will operate effectively within the matter, and there will emerge from it the most pure and red <note>The original text "rubicun-" is a catchword for "rubicundissimum," referring to the *Rubedo* or final reddening stage that signifies the completion of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> gold—

<summary>Morienus explains the central role of the "white smoke" as a spiritual tincture that purifies dark, "dead" matter, restoring its soul and transforming it through stages of whiteness into pure gold.</summary>

WITH ALL possible respects offered to you, venerable Doctor and honored lord. And so it is said that there occurs only a corruption of the form and not a scattering of the matter. If, however, the other grain is cast into fire, then it is corrupted in both its matter and its form, and the whole is scattered—and that corruption is useless for generation. It must be noted, therefore, that the dissolutions of metals occur in different ways. One is that which the fools <note>original: "fatui"; Trevisan frequently uses this term to describe alchemists who follow "vulgar" or incorrect chemical methods.</note> know: as was stated above, using external things that do not remain with the dissolved metals; this is called corrosive destruction and the defiling of the compound <note>original: "compositi"</note>, rather than true dissolution. The second solution is that which occurs by the power and force of fire, which also is not a true solution, but rather a **liquefaction** <term>liquefactio|A physical melting or turning to liquid via heat, which Trevisan distinguishes from a "philosophical" or chemical dissolution.</term> of the elemental parts bound together. For the heat of the fire from without finds the natural or native fire dwelling within the compound, dissolving it; this interior and proportional fire also dwells in the air, and so it dissolves the air itself. That dissolved air then resides and dwells in the water, and the water in the earth, and the water itself dissolves the earth, so that the heat liquefies both the active and the passive parts. But that liquefaction is not a true **dissolution** <term>dissolutio|In alchemy, the process of reducing a solid to its liquid 'prime matter' so it can be reborn.</term>; on the contrary, it is dissipative <note>original: "dissipatiua"</note>, because the elements there are homogeneous to one another, mixed in a fixed proportion through **digestion** <term>digestio|The alchemical process of 'cooking' or maturing the matter through steady, gentle heat to reach perfection.</term>, and one is generally drawn out from the power of the other. And therefore this happens in clean <note>original: "mundis"; referring to purified or refined metals.</note> bodies, in which

### ON THE TRANSMUTATION OF METALS ###

...the elemental natures are fixed. For this reason, within them the flame of fire causes liquefaction, and it dissolves the whole compound into a flow, but not into a separation: because fire cannot flow unless the air substantial to it flows; nor can air flow unless the water is dissolved; nor does water flow unless the earth also flows, and vice versa. Just as earth is dissolved by water, so conversely, water retains and congeals the air; and in the same way, ascending upwards, the air retains the fire in congelation. This occurs because the more **fixed** and **fixing** elements <note>In alchemy, "fixing" refers to the ability of a substance to resist the heat of fire and remain stable.</note>—namely earth and water—acting together, effect a **fixation** <term>fixio|The process by which a substance is made stable in fire so that it no longer evaporates or escapes as vapor.</term>; and conversely, fire and air act together toward dissolution.

But that solution is called the **liquefaction** of the compound, and not properly its dissolution, because the parts are not dissolved from one another as separable units in the generation of the compound—as happens in the **third and true philosophical solution** <note>original: "vera solutione philosophica"</note>. In that true solution, when the compound is dissolved in the aforementioned way, the parts remain unseparated even though they are separable, so that the virtue of the most highly "digested" elements <note>original: "digestissimorum elementorum"; referring to elements that have been matured or refined by heat over time.</note> can be extracted from the things to be dissolved by means of a dissolvent—namely, by **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; while this literally means mercury, Trevisan refers here to a "philosophical" mercury used as a universal solvent.</note>. 

In such a dissolution, the grosser parts take on the "breadth of subtlety": because the **body** is turned into **spirit** <term>spiritus|The volatile, active, or vaporous essence of a substance, as opposed to its solid, "dead" body.</term>, and conversely, the spirit is turned into body; likewise, fixed things are converted into **volatiles**, and volatiles are converted into fixed things. This solution is indeed possible and natural—namely, through the craft administering to nature...

<summary>Trevisan distinguishes between simple melting (liquefaction) and "philosophical solution." He argues that true alchemy requires a total transformation where solids become vapors (spirit) and vapors are stabilized into solids (fixation) using "quicksilver" as a solvent.</summary>

The feminine parts are indeed like **earth and water**, while the masculine parts are like **air and fire**. The philosophers temper this "earth" and "water" of the mercury within the gold, but they described the air and fire within it as being like the **sulfur** <note>In this theory, sulfur is not the yellow chemical element we know today, but a spiritual "fire" or active principle already hidden inside the mercury.</note>. Because of this, the sulfur in gold—namely, the air and fire—is more mature and active in actuality than it is in mercury. For this reason, gold is dissolved by art with mercury, so that the mature might assist the immature. Thus, with art boiling and nature perfecting, the composition is matured, by the grace of Christ. # BERNARDUS TREVISANUS #

...gold is produced more perfectly, more nobly, and in higher degrees than by the work of nature. Because nature only acts and works by cooking and **digesting** <term>digestion|The alchemical process of maturing a substance through steady, gentle heat, mimicking natural processes in the earth.</term> **mercury** <note>original: "Mercurium"</note> alone in the bowels of the earth without any outside help; this cannot reach the proper proportion of gold or any other metal in a short amount of time. 

Our **Art** <note>meaning Alchemy, the "art" of transmuting metals.</note>, however, assists the work of nature by mixing **mature gold** into mercury. In this gold, the **sulfur** <note>original: "sulphur"; the active, "seeding" principle in alchemy.</note> is already perfectly digested, and it therefore matures and quickly digests the mercury itself into the **equal proportion** <note>original: "anaticam... proportionem", likely from the Greek 'ana', meaning equal parts.</note> of gold by refining its elements. From this, a marvelous shortening of this natural work follows through the use of art.

Therefore, my doctor, to return to my previous points, one must not believe the error of those who say that the **masculine agent** <note>The active, "seeding" principle, often identified with Gold or Sulfur.</note> joins the **feminine** <note>The passive, "receiving" principle, identified with Mercury.</note> during the process of thickening, but then departs afterward. For as is well known in all generation, the offspring consists of both the active and the passive. It is necessary for the passive—that is, all four elements—to always remain together; otherwise, no mixing would occur, and the hope of generating an offspring would vanish. 

For in any man, the masculine seed is said to be the active force within him until the end of life, once it is mixed with the feminine seed from the start. If it is poured out or consumed, nature then flourishes, increases marvelously, and is nourished, producing for itself within that same man, in his loins, a similar se- <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing "seed" or "semen" on the next page.</note>

the joining of agents and patients. Yet the philosophers <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers to alchemists, often called "Philosophers of Nature."</note> and ingenious craftsmen, imitating nature, have through most subtle ingenuity made another joining and digestion beyond this natural digestion of seeds in mercury; from which they created not merely simple gold, but something far more noble and perfect. ...foreign to its own nature, because it does not vegetate <note>original: "vegetat"; meaning to grow through a biological, life-sustaining process like a plant</note>. Therefore, although in the said **philosopher's stone** there is a body and a soul or spirit, it is not for that reason vegetatively animated like trees and plants. For this stone, like all minerals, belongs to the aforementioned **first imposition** <note>original: "primæ impositionis"; a term from scholastic philosophy used here to describe the primary level or "order" of natural existence</note>, and not the second, or any higher imposition, as has been said elsewhere. 

Trees and plants, however, belong to the **second imposition**, just as sentient beings belong to the third, fourth, fifth, or the final imposition. For in these four latter impositions, mixed things "vegetate" <note>they possess a life-force that allows for internal growth</note>. In these, the elements—having been altered more often and through more transmutations—are more subtle. For this reason, they are more active and more perfect, although they are not as durable or permanent in their mixture. This is because the elements within them are not of a **fixed composition**, but a resolvable <note>dissolvable or breakable</note> one; therefore, they receive nourishment in a vegetative manner. 

Our **stone**, however, like all minerals, belongs to the first imposition: because it does not vegetate, nor is it nourished vegetatively. Rather, nourishment occurs in it through the **apposition** <note>growth by adding layers to the outside rather than growing from within</note> of a nature similar to itself, and not through biological vegetation. 

For example: as is evident by experiment, this philosopher's stone is nourished by the **feminine seed** <note>original: "spermate fœminino"</note>—namely, by **mercury**—when it is applied to it unitively, imperceptibly, and compositively; this occurs, however, through the mediation of the **digestion of heat**. For it takes to itself its like...

It does not nourish it vegetatively, but through apposition and commingling. 

He, therefore, who multiplies and nourishes the stone in this way will not err, because this multiplying and nourishing substance is converted into the same **species**. However, someone could increase the stone and its weight using foreign things: but this would occur outside of its natural species, and those things would not be convertible into the stone. For that weight would be created contrary to nature; that is, it would not result in the same species or the unity of a single species. ...from every thing, they did not truly understand (as some perversely interpret) that that stone is composed of diverse things dissimilar to itself in both appearance and nature; or (which is even more absurd) that it is multiplied by a flame applied from the outside. They suggest this primarily because fire and its flame could emerge from almost any thing through a certain production <note>i.e., most things can be burned to produce fire</note>; however, the refutation of this opinion is clear from what was said before.

But when the philosophers say that the stone is made from every thing, they mean it is made from the four elements, proportionately **unified** <term>anatizatis; from an alchemical term for the radical blending or "opening" of elements until they are inseparable</term> through proper and natural digestion. It is from these four elements that every thing capable of being generated or corrupted is made. 

Therefore, by this comparison, the philosophers say: our stone is procreated from every thing—that is, from every element—because if one of them were **mortified** <note>original: "mortificato"; rendered inactive or "killed" in a chemical sense</note> or destroyed, the entire proportion of its **golden nature** <term>aureiratis; a specific alchemical term for the essential quality or "goldness" of the substance</term> would perish, as would its very species. 

And although in the entire range and category of changeable things, any object may be generated from the four elements mixed in either act or potentiality, it is not properly said of every such producible thing, but only of our **golden stone** <note>original: "aureo lapide"</note>, or other "unified" things, that it is "made from every thing." This is for the primary reason that in those things produced not by thorough unification <note>original: "anatice"</note> but merely by a balanced proportion of elements, not all elements are present in their actual state, but exist instead in their balanced activity and passivity. For certain...

But in the **Philosopher’s Stone** <term>lapide philosophico; the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold</term>, which is gold (since it is a unified work of nature), all four elements—active and passive—are present in act and remain in equal proportion.

For **goldness** <term>aureitas; the essential, spiritual quality that makes a substance gold</term> is nothing other than the four elements **unified** <term>anatizata; a term derived from the Greek 'ana' (up/throughout), meaning the elements are so thoroughly blended that they act as a single unit</term>. This is not to say that the form and matter are called "unified," but rather the potential and the act. 

That is: they are not unified and equalized by **quantity** (their physical mass), but by **quality**. This is because the active power does not exceed the passive in its action, nor conversely does the passive exceed the active in its suffering <note>original: "patiendo"; in historical physics, 'passion' or 'suffering' is the state of being acted upon by an external force</note>. 

Because there is an equal proportion of measures in gold (or **our medicine** <term>medicina nostra; a common synonym for the Philosopher's Stone, emphasizing its power to 'heal' or perfect base metals</term>): double heat, double moisture, double cold, and double dryness. All of these are present in the very act of doing and being done unto—namely fire, air, water, and earth—as was said before. 

All these things are said to be unified and balanced in quality and not quantity, because they are equally active and passive, and for that reason they remain permanently in gold. Because in gold, the passive resides permanently within the active; and conversely, the passive does not rise up against the active. Nor is it necessary for them to be unified by quantity—that is, that there be just as much of the substance of fire as there is of the substance of earth. For if that were the case, fire, beyond its own quality, would be everywhere, and its activity would not be balanced with the passive earth, but far...

(As is evident to the experienced and the practitioner) when the philosophers said that those three things were present in their Stone of the natural art, they understood them by way of analogy and through practical experiment. For they called the **Body** and its **Bones** "Earth": because it is the binding force of the compound, preventing the fluid elements from their raw state of flux, and possessing within itself "Fire" symbolically in its dryness. However, they called "Water" and "Air" the **Spirit**: because these are the moistening elements that dissolve the Earth.

Furthermore, they called "Air" and "Fire" the **Soul**: because these are the elements that mature and digest <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to a process of slow, constant heat that matures a substance.</note> the entire compound. And so they named these things according to the human likeness. For just as in the complexioned flesh there must be bones supporting the body, and in the flesh there must likewise be the vitality of the vegetative properties, which are called its "spirits"—contrary to the errors of the pagan philosophers, who thought the vital spirits were something distinct from the composite body and its components—so too in human flesh there must be an "informative soul" <note>original: "animam informatiuam," a Scholastic term for the soul that gives form and life to matter.</note> digesting the animal impulses within a man and performing in him the intellectual work.

But in our **Philosophical Stone**, it must be understood differently: in the Stone, "Earth" bears the name of "Bones"; "Water" and "Air" obtain the name of "Spirit"; nor is there a "Soul" within it, except insofar as it contains Air and Fire. The philosophers have divided this matter. For by means of a raw spirit <note>original: "spiritum crudum"; in alchemy, a "spirit" refers to a volatile substance that can be vaporized</note>, they extracted a digested spirit from the dissolved body, and there remained for them a fixed ash <note>The solid residue left after heating</note> to be further dissolved, in which they found an oiliness and a stony, incombustible gumminess, which they called the **soul**. It is otherwise in gold, in which whatever is within it is found to be of a single species. Therefore, my venerable Doctor, the philosophers say this by way of analogy for the sake of the administration of the art and the operation of nature: not because there is a soul in the stone, except metaphorically (as you skillfully understand), nor a spirit, nor a body, in the sense of a "formable" form as is found in man and other sentient beings. Would Josephus <note>Likely referring to an alchemical authority cited by the correspondent, possibly Josephus Agricola or a pseudo-epigraphical source</note> say that mercury, or any other of the metals, could be changed in its internal quality or nature by simple water—no matter how hot and boiling—or that it could acquire its natural moisture and thus be "revivified" <note>The process of restoring liquid mercury from a solid salt or precipitate</note>? Therefore, the earth of the bodies [requires] the calcination <note>A process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to achieve decomposition or oxidation.</note> of the copper, so that it may be most excellently purified from false sulfurous qualities and combustions. Therefore, it is established that if the corruptible matter had not then been placed there through the corruption of the stone, it would never be necessary for it to be cleansed.

And since it is thus necessary that, after the corruption of the stone, the compound of the stone itself be purified of all its filth—following its separation through the four elements by means of distillation and calcination—before the Mercury <note>In alchemy, "Mercury" often refers to the "spirit" or the transformative principle of a substance, rather than just the common metal.</note> is joined with the body to begin the real preparation, which is the creation of our stone.

For this reason, it is necessary that the stone be divided through the four elements with distillation and calcination. And this division is solely so that the substance of the stone may be powerfully clean, and that the whole may be pure Mercury, which carries within itself the property of melting and fixing <note>Fixing refers to making a volatile substance stable and resistant to fire.</note>. ### PHILOSOPHY 117

<margin>Book 11</margin>
The matter of dissolution <note>original: "dissolutionis"; the process of breaking a solid down into liquid</note> is that which occurs with the congealing of the spirit, and cannot happen without it. However, do not assume that the separation of the elements occurs, or can even be possible, except through putrefaction <note>the breaking down of organic or chemical matter through heat and moisture</note>. It is through this process that the spirit is mixed into the body and with its elements; and it is this which renders them volatile <note>able to evaporate or rise as vapor</note>, as is apparent in their separations. Therefore, digest and putrefy the elements in their own dregs <note>original: "simis"; likely referring to the sediment or "slime" of the matter</note> until the end. When this has been well-digested to satisfy our will, so that it can be properly separated, then bury it <note>original: "inhuma"; to place the vessel in a warm "earth" or sand bath</note> so that the separated thing can be better purified, and become quicksilver <note>mercury</note> in the form of clear water.

But if you do not divide the stone—namely, the fifth essence <note>the "quintessence" or purest state of matter beyond the four elements</note>—through the four elements, know that it cannot be naturally united, nor joined with the dry body, unless each of them holds something of the nature of the fifth essence. For that essence is the mixing of all elements and their reduction into one pure substance. It is necessary that those elements be well-purified from their infections <note>impurities or taints</note>. And we tell you that the combustible sulfurous qualities <note>original: "sulphureitates"; the flammable principle in alchemy</note> should be separated through the benefit of calcination <note>reduction to ash by high heat</note>, and be totally annihilated from the fire and from the earth. Let the body be broken down and greatly refined through such digestion, and let the waters be thoroughly purified from their filth with distillations and by refining.

...they may be turned into the nature of the air, through the smoothing process of lightness <note>original: "levigationem levitatis," referring to the process of grinding a substance into a fine, light powder</note>. Then you are able to perform the **union of the male with the female**, so that between themselves they may beget the **son of fire**, who is so greatly desired by the love of all philosophers. And here it must be noted, that in the hidden part <note>the "occult" or internal essence</note> of our stone there is heat and dryness, and in the manifest part <note>the "manifest" or outward appearance</note> there is coldness and moisture: wherefore it is necessary to hide its manifest part, and to make manifest its hidden part. This is because the heat which is in the hidden part is the element, and the oil is also dry. For this dryness fixes the substance, since the dryness of the fire provides the tint <note>original: "tingit," the power to transform or color other metals</note>.

However, that which is in the manifest part is coldness and moisture. It is necessary, therefore, to have a proportion between these, so that the coldness and moisture may be tempered by the heat and dryness, in such a way that they do not flee from the fire. Act, therefore, so that the moisture and coldness receive the heat and dryness which were in the hidden part, so that they may become one single substance.

Indeed, that coldness and moisture is a watery and scorching smoke, which corrupts and gives birth to blackness <note>the "nigredo" stage of alchemy, representing decay before rebirth</note>. And that stone is of one virtue and nature in its hidden part, and of another in its manifest part: but in a complete mixture, it is of the same virtue and nature: and thus the species is changed into a **most noble body**. Then it becomes flowing like oil, which is a living tincture, capable of multiplication and consolidation.

### PHILOSOPHY.
To bury <note>original: "Abſqere" (likely a variant of "inhumare")</note> is to inter, to distill, to ascend and to descend. To join is to impregnate, to whiten, and to redden. To fix, however, is to ferment and to betroth <note>original: "deſponſare"; a metaphor for the chemical union of substances</note>. Solution converts the stone into its first matter, that is, its water; absolution <note>original: "abſolutio"; here meaning a loosening or release of vapors</note> into air; conjunction into fire; and fixation into a spiritual and dyeing earth.
Wherefore Aristotle <note>A common attribution in medieval alchemy, though often referring to pseudo-Aristotelian texts</note> says: When you have water from air, and air from fire, and fire from earth, then you shall have the full art. Because the four elements are then well and perfectly prepared, and the master of the work and the fire performs all these things well in one single vessel, in four stages—namely, the four types of colors of conversion, as shall be spoken of within.

Fire, according to Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose medical and alchemical theories were foundational in Europe</note>, is dissolved so that it may be converted into Mercury, and divided into the four elements, so that it may have its first origin; and so that the sulfur of the philosophers may be extracted from the body, and pure quicksilver <term>argentum vivum: literally "living silver," the liquid metal mercury</term> may be obtained upon the earth, from that matter out of which gold and silver are made beneath the earth. And let those things be cooked together until they become one: stable, penetrating, and deep-reaching, dyeing and permanent. One part of this converts a thousand thousand parts of Mercury, or of any imperfect body, into the truest gold or silver, according to how the Elixir was prepared. And at this, Richard <note>Likely referring to Richardus Anglicus, a 13th-century alchemist</note> marveled...

For thus says Geber: "Where we have spoken most openly and plainly, there we most conceal our science."

# PHILOSOPHY

There is but one stone; if anyone wanders from that one in the beginning, they will be rewarded with weariness in the end. <note>The author emphasizes that alchemy requires a single starting material; starting with the wrong substance leads to failure and exhaustion.</note>

However, this "one" is not one in number, but in kind. Just as a male and a female are sufficient for procreating offspring without any other addition, so too the Stone of the Philosophers <note>original: "lapis philosophorum"</note>, composed of two, is sufficient for the intended medicine—namely, the spirit and the soul, which are the Sun and the Moon <note>In alchemy, the Sun (Sol) represents Gold or the masculine principle, while the Moon (Luna) represents Silver or the feminine principle.</note>. 

And some say that to these two a third should be added, namely the body. For just as a human being consists of body, soul, and spirit, so too does our Stone. In this matter, however, there are diverse opinions: for some say that one of these two is both spirit and body, and they deceive people regarding the addition of a third. Others say that the "third" is simply the name for the composite made of the two, because it resembles neither of the components individually, and it is called by the name "of all bodies" <note>original: "omnicorporum"</note>. Others say that a body must truly be joined to these two, because the work will be stronger, and their operation will be finished in a short time. 

But whichever opinion is held, the number is not increased. For the sake of clarity, it should be noted that *Kibric* <note>A term derived from the Arabic 'Kibrit,' meaning Sulfur.</note> is the father of Mercury and of all liquefiable things. And this is said to be that "one thing" which is both precious and vile. Quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum," referring to Mercury</note>, however, is its son, although it is different and foreign from it in its temperament; and thus it stands, just as a father...

In the first stage of governance, when it is black, it is called **earth**, and **Saturn**, and by the names of all black and earthly bodies. This spirituality, or earth, is called our **bronze** and our **lead**. It is necessary, therefore, to govern it gently, so that the sulfur may become unburnable <note>original: "incremabile"; meaning it can withstand the fire without being consumed</note> along with the water in which it resides. Therefore, heaven must be repeated over the earth so many times until the earth becomes heavenly and spiritual, and the heaven becomes earthly and is joined with the earth; then it is completed.

# PHILOSOPHY

The work is fulfilled. And it must be known that since the body is coarse and the spirit is subtle, they cannot be mixed together universally unless the body is first made so subtle by the spirit that the body itself equals the spirit in its fineness. Only then does such a mixture occur that fire cannot separate or overcome it, even if it were to act upon it continuously for a thousand years. This is because they are mixed through their smallest parts <note>Latin: "per minima," a term in natural philosophy referring to the smallest possible units of matter</note> so that by no ingenuity can they be separated once they have taken hold of one another. For if the dragon shall die, it is not without the other—that is, unless it is killed along with it. And this dragon, which is sulfur, is extracted from the body through the mastery of the art <term>magisterium: the skilled process of alchemical transformation</term>, and it is our secret sulfur.

Therefore, when you wish to test the medicine, place the weight of one grain of wheat upon a glowing plate of copper. If, upon entering with a little heat, the plate spreads the medicine throughout, both inside and out, it is perfectly penetrating <note>Latin: "ungens," literally 'anointing' or 'smearing,' referring here to the medicine's ability to flow and permeate the metal</note>. If it perseveres in the fire, it is the Stone; then it is perfect. And so it is clear that there are three things which complete our Elixir that we have made: the first joins them, and the two compose the medicine. Thus, there are three joined in one body.

But it should be noted that if the medicine is dissolved again and guided through all the steps as before, there will be no end to its power of staining <term>tinctura: the ability of the alchemist's stone to change the color and nature of metals</term>. It constricts the pores of the Moon <note>The alchemical name for Silver</note>, making it heavy, and in other bodies, it will cause the dross and foam to be cast out.

## PHILOSOPHY

The neutrality of the extremes belongs to the philosophers <note>original: "philosophis"; referring to the alchemists or "natural philosophers"</note>, because it is said that the seed of metals is contained within the womb of the earth. One extreme side of this, below, is the metal which is created by nature at the ends of the earth; the other extreme side, above, is the completed elixir <note>term: elixir; the perfected substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold</note>, through which art works upon the earth by mediating nature.

And there is no passage from one extreme to the other except through a midpoint. Therefore, it is necessary that neutrality be sought so that a body may be reduced to its center by art. This art imitates nature as much as it can; however, in certain respects it is weaker, and in others, it corrects nature.

From this, it should be known that the intention of our transformation is to begin where nature has finished. This is because the origin of nature's work regarding all homogeneous things <note>substances of the same kind or uniform structure</note> is internally watery, and extends divisibly to three degrees of extremity: namely, to the height of perfected bodies, or the depth of the perfected, or to the breadth of their neutrality—specifically by quickening the dead and killing the living, whose quickening is death-bearing.

Hence the Philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle, often cited as "The Philosopher" in medieval texts</note> says: Every whole is composed of three parts, around which the work of nature can exist. First, to elicit the natures, to collect them, to purify them, and to join them proportionally in a watery form, and furthermore to congeal them, so that from the moisture...

# PHILOSOPHY
## The second step of the Ladder of the Wise is Solution.

Which is the revelation of the hidden, the thinning of coarseness, and the reduction of a hard thing—dry earth—into a certain liquid substance. Whence the philosopher <note>Likely referring to Aristotle or a foundational alchemical authority</note> says: *Until all things become water, you shall work nothing.* <note>original: "Donec omnia fiant aqua nihil operamini"</note> And that water is the **Mercury of the Philosophers**, which we must use and no other; yet it does not exist until the sum of the volatile overcomes the sum of the fixed. This water, according to Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy</note>, the father of philosophers, is called "the unique" from repugnant things, and **Magnesia**, containing in itself the spirit, soul, and body of the ash. It is unequal in its name because nothing is similar to it, and it is fitting for it to manifest the hidden nature: its secret is not in others, because according to the philosophers it is called **celestial water**, and there are repugnant things in this one water. Therefore, convert thing into thing, and you shall have the mastery. And in this solution, while the earth is disturbed, the mountains shall be carried into the heart of the sea <note>A metaphorical description of the solid matter dissolving into the liquid solvent</note>, and then the form is destroyed; but one being destroyed, another is immediately introduced. Because every quality arriving at a quality makes it such as it was not before, for it is not possible to give a natural quality unless it remains under some form, containing in itself qualities in act or in potentiality.

Wherefore Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, the Persian physician and philosopher whose works were central to medieval alchemy</note> says: The quality after—

The former draws its <term>entity</term><note>Latin: entitatem; the essential being or substance of a thing</note> from the <term>quality</term><note>Latin: qualitate; the specific properties or characteristics</note> which is its prior.

The **dissolution of the stone**, however, is its reduction into the **mineral water** from which it was composed by the working of nature. Indeed, this stone does not bear fruit until it comes to nothing, like running water. Therefore, since it is fitting for this reduction to take place by dissolving it, it is easier and more suitable to reduce it first to a state of neutrality, and afterwards to its primary watery nature, or otherwise finally to some other subtlety. And what can be done through fewer means is done in vain through many. Wherefore the **Philosopher** <note>Likely referring to Aristotle, often cited as "The Philosopher" in medieval texts</note> says: "If you can achieve perfection from **Mercury** alone, you will be an investigator of the most precious work." And know that it is not a foreign thing into which it must be converted through the natural mastery, just as is evident with frozen ice, which, when it is resolved, is turned into water; it is evident, therefore, that it was water beforehand. Wherefore he says: "Unless everything is turned into water, perfection will in no way be reached." Whence **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says: "Nature is not improved except in its own nature," the improvement of which nature is done by the ingenuity of art, and art does not correct in nature what nature cannot do. Nature must therefore be aided by art in that which was omitted by nature. For that which nature is only able to perfect below in terms of thousands of years, we, by the industry of the highest art, in a shorter term—

In a set limit of time rather than in a single year, we are able to complete that which is more than perfect; and thus nature is aided by the intellect <note>original: "ingenio"</note>, and the intellect by art.

For Aristotle says: "Unless I saw gold and silver, I would say for certain that alchemy was not true; unless I saw the perfection of nature's work through speculation, I would not consider alchemy to be true."

It must be known that there are many modes of solutions <note>The process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state, a key stage in the Great Work</note>, yet of all these, only one solution is necessary for us, which is only to be made—as I have said—from itself with itself, etc.; raw, clear, and without violence.

Whence the philosopher says: A raw solution is better than a cooked one, dewy better than dry, voluntary better than forced, tempered better than hasty, flaming <note>original: "flaqra," likely "flagra," referring to a bright or burning quality</note> better than foul-smelling, clear better than thick, and black better than red.

And therefore, in every solution, one must inwardly beware of the vitrification <note>The turning of the matter into a glass-like, inert substance</note> of the matter along with the odors and tastes of imperfect bodies, and also lest the generative power of that form be in any way suffocated by burning corrosives. And our digestion is called: the thinning of the humor, a destructive ripening, a relaxation of things bound together, an awakening of disposition, and a separation—

## The Third Step of the Ladder of the Sages.

The aforementioned four clashing elements, having been distinguished from one another, are afterwards separated in this third step of the Ladder of the Sages through a rectifying distillation: and for that reason, this step is called our "separation." This is the separation of the watery or liquid-like vapor from the dregs; or rather, it is a purification, a smoothing of the thinness, an extraction of the coarse parts, a division of those things joined together, a production of first principles, and a segregation of like-substances.

Hence the Psalm says: *He brought water out of the rock, and oil out of the hardest stone.* <note>original: "Eduxit aquam de petra, & oleum de faxo durissimo." A paraphrase of Psalm 78:16 and Deuteronomy 32:13, used here to symbolize extracting the essence from base matter.</note> This must be done in the proper baths <term>balneis: water-baths or "bains-marie" used for gentle heating</term>, and afterwards in dry stoves <term>stufis siccis: dry heat chambers or ovens</term>, according to the requirements of reason. From these, first their dross <term>stegma: a term for mineral refuse or slag</term> is separated and emptied out in the baths. Then these four principles are separated according to the required signs from the beginning, and especially the Moon <note>In alchemy, "Moon" (Luna) usually refers to Silver or the feminine principle</note>, the male prior to the female, and thus with their mother left at the bottom in the first distillation—namely, you will keep the lemon-colored sapphire <note>original: "saphiram citrinam," likely referring to a yellow-tinted liquid or "oil" produced in the vessel</note>—afterwards the orpiment <term>auripigmentum: arsenic trisulfide, a yellow mineral</term>, as much from the moisture as by itself, so many times in a dry stove—

### *The fourth step of our scale of wisdom*
### *is, and is called, Conjunction.*

Therefore, once the four distinct elements have been separated as previously mentioned and rectified <note><term>rectified</term> purified through repeated distillation</note>, we join and connect those same four: and our conjunction is called a mixing of qualities, a coupling of those embracing, a folding back of things dispersed, an equalization of principles, and an arrangement of things in opposition. For the *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise</note> says: *Arrange the airy substance* through discernment, so that the earth may be held from two natures, and the water, as predicted, from two bodies: because in this way the subtle is separated from the coarse, and the rare from the dense. For no water is necessary for our work except that which is bright; nor any oil, except that which is white and clear of yellowness; nor any earth, except that which is pale and whitish: because then the earth is fit for binding, the water for dissolving, and the air is superabundant for tinting.

An example of this is the work of the potter, whose reliability consists in two things, namely the dry and the moist: the dry so that it may convert the moist, and the moist so that it may dissolve the dry; and thus, with the spirit mixed with the body, there is a temperament, neither so rare as the spirit, nor so dense as the body. For **dissolving and joining** are the principal elements of this art, and the beginnings of the work, and a single power. For he who does not dissolve and coagulate, errs manifoldly.

*The fifth step of our Scale is, and*
*it is called Putrefaction.*

Which is celebrated for forty-six nights in the **shadow of purgatory** <note>A metaphorical term for the dark, transitional stage of the alchemical process where the matter "dies" to be reborn</note>. And putrefaction is necessary: because it is the corruption <note>In the Aristotelian sense: the breakdown of one form to allow for the generation of another</note> and the beginning of regeneration.

And know that the air extended between heaven and earth, through which the life of every single thing exists, runs over all four natures in their manifest and hidden states. Know also, that this preparation of conversion is effected from thing to thing, and from state to state.

### PHILOSOPHY

<margin><unclear>concerning</unclear></margin>
It is said that just as the seed of man is transformed alone in the womb through a natural preparation from one state to another, until a perfect human is formed from it—which was its root and beginning—it does not change away from this, nor does it depart from its own root by dividing from one thing into another. This occurs through the entry of another substance upon it, namely the menstrual blood <note>The author is using the Aristotelian theory of embryology, where the male seed provides the form and the female blood provides the material matter.</note>, from which the seed was formed; that is, from a blood similar to it, which served as its nourishment. Similarly, all things develop without the entry of any other external thing upon them, except for a preservative and nutritive heat which enters into it. Thus it is transformed from state to state, and is divided from one thing to another, becoming a chick flying from the nest. And just as that from which it had its root and beginning, so also the seeds of all things growing from the earth undergo putrefaction <note>term: putrefaction (the breaking down or "death" of a substance required before a new form can arise)</note> and are changed through the entry of corruption upon them. Then they sprout and increase, just like those things from which they had their root. And for this reason, minerals are not nourished in a way that they depart from their own root; rather, the body returns to that from which it was, nor is it converted into anything else regarding the conception and the extraction of the spirit. This is like the discharge of the woman's blood, which is called the menses, with which the fetus, as long as it is in the womb, must alone be fed: because at the time of the putrefaction of this fetus, nothing of it will be visible. For your Sun <note>original: "Sol"; likely referring to the alchemical gold or the masculine principle</note> goes toward the northern part, and the water which comes out of the woman is then rightly called

# THE LADDER

<term>menstruum</term> <note>original: "menstruum"; in alchemy, this refers to a universal solvent or "mother" liquid that dissolves solids, named after the monthly cycle believed to nourish an embryo</note>: because with it and in it, the <term>menstrual blood</term> <note>original: "sanguis menstrualis"; here used as a metaphor for the raw, undigested material of the Great Work</note> not yet well-digested <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the slow heating of a substance to mature it</note> departs from the body; and it is that pure essence which first illuminated it, which it received from the Sun, which is its life after its death, and which also begins to depart from it in the first <term>solution</term> <note>the process of turning a solid into a liquid</note>. Its color is green, on account of the abundance of the soul's coldness: and thus the "menstruum" is the name given to the water with which the <term>compound</term> <note>the mixture of alchemical ingredients</note> shall be managed during the first three months.

But when the <term>fetus</term> <note>the developing alchemical Stone</note> begins to be quickened with life, it draws this menstruum into its body little by little, until it is drawn away from the womb, and this occurs through the passage to the navel, and thus it is brought forth into the light. For the menstruum is blood not well-digested; because of a lack of heat, that which is well-digested is converted into milk, which is called the **crown**. From this it is clear that it is blood twice-cooked.

And you should know that our sharp, fiery water is the "menstruous water," then four parts of the first <term>lime</term> <note>original: "calcis"; the powdered residue left after heating a substance to high temperatures</note> are dissolved within; when its four congealed natures are applied, it suddenly blackens everything through <term>putrefaction</term> <note>the stage of decay or "death" of the matter, usually resulting in a black color called the nigredo</note>. This is the "second water" of which the *Rosary* <note>original: "Rosarius"; likely referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise</note> speaks, saying: "Our water is to be divided into two parts, by one part of which the body is congealed—namely, with its seven soakings and congealings—but by the other part it putrefies and is melted like the fiery water mentioned above."

<header>PHILOSOPHY</header>

<margin>What the stone is</margin>
Now, by this sublimation <note>original: "sublimationem"; the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then solidifies again to purify it</note> is understood the preparation of the stone, and the seed of perfect union with itself.

<margin>What the medicine is</margin>
Then it is also a simple medicine, but not yet perfected, nor at its highest state of perfection, until the medicine is ennobled through exaltation <note>original: "exaltationem"; a process intended to increase the "virtue" or potency of a substance</note> and raised up, as will appear below.

<margin>Four causes of sublimation</margin>
And it must be known that we perform sublimation for four reasons.

<margin>The first cause</margin>
First, so that the body may become a spirit of subtle matter.

<margin>The second cause</margin>
Second, so that Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius"; often referring to Quicksilver or the philosophical principle of fluidity and transformation</note> may incorporate itself with the body and become one with it.

<margin>The third cause</margin>
Third, so that the whole may become white, and then red and pure, and the falseness of the sulfur <note>original: "sulphuris"; in alchemy, sulfur often represents the active, combustible principle which must be purified of "falseness" or impurities</note> may be diminished; and especially so that the innate moisture of the stone may be restored—which it first lost when reduced to lime <note>original: "calce"; the powdery residue left after a substance has been burned or calcined</note>—and that it may be prepared for the swiftest liquefaction. For the medicine must be a simple powder of the most subtle and pure substance, adhering to quicksilver <note>original: "argento viuo"</note> by its very nature, and of the easiest liquefaction, hidden refinement, and the thinnest penetration like water, remaining fixed against the struggle of the fire before the flight of Mercury. Then, whatever is added to it will be of the same temperament <note>original: "complexionis"</note> as that to which it is added: so that if you add water to it, the whole will be dissolved into water; but if you place it in fire, the whole will become fire. And when you have fixed the Elixir, you should bring back the apparatus over it.

And it must be known, that every dissolution <note>original: "dissolutio"; the process of breaking a solid down into a liquid state</note> occurs according to a natural affinity: for everything that dissolves the moon <note>The alchemical symbol for Silver</note>, also dissolves the sun <note>The alchemical symbol for Gold</note>, because the body is extremely hot, and nothing can penetrate it except the most subtle spirit, which is also called "air." Wherefore it is clear, that through quicksilver <note>mercury</note> it does not coagulate the white <term>white: the "albedo" stage of the Great Work</term> while enduring the fire, and it does not join with pure silver, nor does it require anything for whiteness: and the same applies to pure gold regarding the red <term>red: the "rubedo" or final stage of the Great Work</term>: because it will profit neither itself, nor another, nor the world. Yet the operation of both is one and the same, except that the white work is the work of winter, as I have said, and the red is of summer: hence in the time of summer, and of the floods, the inundation of waters corrupts the **third mastery** <note>the third stage of the alchemical process</note>.

The Sun <note>Gold</note> does not tint, as I said before, unless it is tinted, nor does it tint unto completion, unless it is more fully dissolved. Moreover, it is fully dissolved if they are fixed into the fourth degree through sublimation. And thus it is evident that without **ferment**, neither the Sun nor the Moon will emerge.

<note>The marginalia appear to be repetitive shorthand notes—likely "minor" and "mensura" (measure)—used by a student or reader to track a logical argument about the smallest possible parts of a substance.</note>

The philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle</note> argues that in every natural thing, there is a limit to how large or small it can be. Just as there is a maximum size for a human being or a tree, there must also be a <term>minimum natural part</term> <note>original: "minimum naturale"; the smallest unit of a substance that still retains its specific properties</note>. If a substance is divided beyond this point, it ceases to be that substance and becomes something else.

Furthermore, he posits that quantity is not merely a mathematical abstraction but is tied to the very essence of the material. If we consider the <term>continuum</term> <note>a mathematical or physical structure where points are connected without gaps</note>, we must ask whether it is composed of indivisible points or of parts that are always further divisible. 

<column-break/>

In this section, the distinction is made between mathematical division, which can proceed to infinity, and physical division, which is limited by the requirements of the <term>form</term> <note>the organizing principle that makes a thing what it is</note>. For example, a single drop of water can be divided, but eventually, one reaches a "minor" part that can no longer function as water if split again.

This leads to the conclusion that "such a measure" <note>original: "talis mensura"</note> is necessary for the existence of natural bodies. Without these boundaries of "minor" and "major," the physical world would lack stable identities, dissolving into an infinite flux of quantity without quality.

<summary>This page discusses the philosophical concept of "minima naturalia," arguing that physical substances have a minimum size limit required to maintain their identity. It contrasts infinite mathematical divisibility with the practical limits of physical matter.</summary>
<keywords>natural philosophy, minima naturalia, divisibility, continuum, Aristotle, physics, quantity, substance</keywords>

->Water is next to air below, just as air is next to fire above; therefore, water is contrary to fire, just as earth is to air, because water and air agree in moisture, while fire and earth agree in dryness.<-

Earth is immediately changed into fire, just as water is changed into air; but fire and water, or air and earth, do not rotate <note>The "rotation of the elements" is a core alchemical concept where one substance is refined into another by cycling through their qualities.</note> unless the earth is first converted into water and the air into fire. Indeed, fire in its highest altitude, according to Roger Bacon <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292) was an English philosopher and friar who was a major authority in medieval alchemy.</note>, is naturally hot and dry in the fourth degree. If you wish to turn this into water, you must reduce the body to a balanced state <term>temperamentum: a state of equilibrium between opposing qualities</term> so that it becomes receptive; reduce it into lime <note>original: "calcem" – referring to calcination, the process of heating a substance until it becomes a powder</note>, then to fire, and then water must be applied, which is cold and moist. However, in the fourth degree, there is a balance that is neither hot nor cold; and thus water, when mixed with fire, creates a balance that is neither moist nor dry.

In the same way, by means of qualities that diminish or increase, earth and air are brought to a state of balance; and so, when the spirit is mixed with the body, as I have said before, a balance is created that is not as thin as spirit, nor as dense as the body.

Furthermore, when you are engaged in the work, strive to record in your mind all the signs of nature which appear in every decoction <note>The process of heating or "cooking" the alchemical matter</note>, and investigate their causes. If the work is brought to the final red state <note>original: "statum rubeum finalem"</note> before the proper end of the whiteness has been reached in administering the process, you must conclude that you have erred corruptively—which God forbid.
