Keep it always lukewarm until it rots continually and is made black once again. Beware especially of that redness because of the danger it poses.

The sign of the first perfect whiteness—that is, of the whole material—is the appearance of a certain small hair-like circle. This appears around the material along the sides of the vessel, being somewhat yellowish <note>original: "subcitrini"</note>, where previously, after the deepest blackness, a white circle had appeared. Do not care about the colors appearing before the true whiteness, because they are not true. For the matter becomes black twice, becomes vile twice, becomes white twice, and becomes red twice.

For when it is composed and putrefied for four days, it will give a dark black color that will remain for a long time; secondly, a yellowish-black; thirdly, a reddish-black; fourthly, a red similar to clear, dry saffron; and fifthly, finally, the heat of true whiteness, around which you will achieve no further effect <note>meaning the stage is stable</note>. However, when it appears glowing white throughout the whole material, like foliated earth <note>term: "terra foliata" - a flaky, crystalline state of the alchemical matter</note> or red leaves, fix it firmly and calcine it <note>term: "calcina" - to reduce to powder through dry heat</note>. Then, by adding new moisture <note>original: "humorem"</note>, exalt it, and fix it again, and do this repeatedly. Finally, having extinguished the fire as previously stated, continually exalt the whiteness.

## *The eleventh step is called multiplication.*

Which is the increase of goodness, the exaltation of color, and the skillful accumulation of infinite quantity.

And this is the reason why our medicine must be able to be multiplied unto infinity. For the medicine itself is like fire within wood, and like musk among fine spices. Therefore, it grows the more it is trodden upon by use: for which reason you must leave a part of it at all times, since you are enriched three times over by it, just as he who possesses fire is enriched by fire.

Moreover, the medicine can be multiplied in two ways. First, through <term>solution</term><note>The process of dissolving a solid into liquid</note> and repeated <term>coagulation</term><note>The process of thickening or solidifying a liquid</note>, and this is its virtual multiplication in quality or "goodness."

The second is through <term>fermentation</term>, and this is its multiplication in quantity. However, you will accomplish the increase through fermentation more quickly, because that which is dissolved does not work well unless...

## An epilogue of the whole, and a summary recapitulation of all things said above.

Therefore, let the Stone be taken—which is sufficiently known from the previous chapters—and with the urgency of the work, let the perfection of sublimation be applied assiduously upon it. Because the white work belongs to winter, and the red work belongs to summer; and therefore, it requires a greater refinement of its parts through its own proper methods in a greater decoction <note>boiling or heating</note> of digestion, namely, until it becomes most red...

### *On the division of the stone into four elements. And how the property of every element existing in the stone is divided into four elements.*

**John of Austria** <note>original: "Iohannes Austri" - a philosopher frequently cited in alchemical anthologies like the 'Theatrum Chemicum'.</note> the philosopher says: Every body is either an element, or it is composed of elements. But every composition and generation consists of the four simple elements. Therefore, it is necessarily required that our **stone** <term>lapis: the "Philosophers' Stone," the goal of the alchemical work</term> be reduced to the **primary matter** <term>materia prima: the formless, original substance from which all things are created</term> and to the origin of **sulfur** and **Mercury** <note>In alchemy, these represent the active/combustible and passive/fluid principles rather than common chemicals.</note>. Then let it be divided into elements, otherwise it cannot be purified, nor ground down, nor can its parts enter into one another at all, unless its body has been divided into the smallest possible parts.

For then its parts may be well purified, and through common properties they are well joined, and the **elixir** <term>elixir: the perfected substance capable of transmuting metals or healing</term> which is sought is produced. For the **chemical operation** <note>original: "experimentum"</note> destroys its specific form and introduces a new species. Hence, after the division of the elements, nothing of them is seen or touched except **water** and **earth**: because **air** and **fire** are never seen in our stone, nor are their virtues felt, except in the purer elements, because they have been made subtle and simple, so that they cannot be seen with physical eyes. Therefore, that stone thus extracted is sufficient for you, so that you may reduce it to the simple effect of its virtue.

Likewise, there are four elements in it, namely fire,

Fire, air, water, and earth. In these are four principles or qualities: namely hot, moist, cold, and dry. Of these principles, two are friendly and two are enemies. Likewise, two are **active** and two are **passive**. Two ascend, and the other two descend. One is in the middle, and another is below that. And the reason for this is that a contrary is not united with its contrary except through a **medium** <term>medium: a middle substance or quality that shares traits with two opposing things, allowing them to join</term>. Therefore, that which is not contrary by its own nature is already united.

Just as hot and dry are united by their nature, since they are in no way contrary to each other; for those two elements, fire and air, are easily joined together by themselves. But hot and cold are not united except through a medium, namely through the moist and the dry: because they cannot stand together by themselves, since one is always contrary to the other. 

For moist and cold exist well together, but hot and cold gather and scatter **homogeneous** things <term>homogenia: substances of the same kind or uniform nature</term>, and not **heterogeneous** <term>eterogenia: substances made of different or unrelated parts</term>, by dissolving and congealing. But moist and dry are gathered and scattered by binding and moistening. 

The operation of the elements is therefore a simple generation and a natural transformation. Thus it is manifest that all things are changed through heat and cold, and are simply generated and naturally transformed. For heat and cold give life to matter; but when the active forces are overcome, it is clear how according to the par-

It presses down and makes compact that which is thin and soft.

As for the earth, I do not care what its color or substance may be, so long as it is **subtle** <note>refined to a very fine or "spirit-like" state</note>, clear, and **fixed** <term>Fixation: the process of making a substance stable so that it no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to heat</term>, etc.

### *Concerning the true philosophical putrefaction of our stone.*

**Arnoldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist</note> says in his **Rosary** <note>original: *Rosario* — referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a seminal alchemical treatise</note>: In our work, **putrefaction** <term>Putrefaction: the "blackening" stage (Nigredo) where the matter is broken down, often compared to a seed rotting in the earth before it can sprout</term> is necessary, because nothing is ever born, or grows, or is given life, except after putrefaction. For if the matter is not putrefied, it can neither be melted nor dissolved. And if it is not dissolved, it will be reduced to nothing.

<summary>This page explains that while pure elements only exist in their ideal spheres, their qualities can be separated in the laboratory, concluding with the necessity of "putrefaction" (the breaking down of matter) as a prerequisite for any alchemical growth.</summary>

Therefore, **our putrefaction** <term>Putrefaction: in alchemy, this is not the rotting of organic matter, but a stage of breakdown and fermentation where the "body" of the metal is softened and blackened to prepare it for rebirth</term> is not filthy or unclean, but is a mixture of water with earth, and earth with water, down to the **smallest parts** <note>original: *minima* — refers to the corpuscular or atomic level</note>, until the whole body becomes one. Hence, Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist, said to be the teacher of the King Khalid (Hali)</note> the philosopher says: In the putrefaction of our **bronze** <note>original: *aeris* — while literally "bronze" or "copper," it represents the base metallic matter of the work</note>, the spirits are united with the body and are dried out within it. Furthermore, our putrefaction is nothing other than the **mortification** <note>The "killing" or neutralizing of a substance's original properties so it can take on new ones</note> of the moist with the dry. And our putrefaction does not happen without the moist and the dry, because the earth is contained in dryness, and it cannot rise by itself. The reason: because heavy things cannot ascend higher, nor can light things remain lower with heavy ones and be thrust down without their fellowship, but each is the beginning and the end of the other.

Hence King Hali <note>Khalid ibn Yazid, an Umayyad prince and famous figure in early alchemy</note> says: Know that unless you have **sublimated** <term>Sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used here to mean refining the matter into a "spiritual" state</term> the body until it becomes water, the water will not putrefy in its entirety; nor can it be congealed, except by fire. For fire congeals the mixture of our stone. And likewise, we dissolve the bodies so that the heat may adhere to their innermost depths. and thus fire alone changes the water and the earth from their natures and colors.

## *Again, concerning the natural, reciprocal, and circular proximity of the elements to one another.*

**Albertus Magnus** <note>original: "Albertus Magnus" — a 13th-century scholar and bishop who was legendary in the Middle Ages for his supposed mastery of alchemy and the natural sciences.</note> says: It must not be passed over in silence that among all things which are related to one another in a circle through generation, their transition is easier because they share common ground in many respects.

This is why gold is more easily made from **silver** than from any other metal. Nature has therefore arranged things well, so that the elements communicate their qualities to one another in a circle, so that circular **transmutations** <term>transmutationes</term> <note>the process of changing one substance into another, such as lead into gold</note> might be made from them, and would result from the circular changing of the elements. For example, **earth** communicates its dryness to **fire**, fire communicates its heat to **air**, air its moisture to **water**, while water communicates its coldness to earth, and earth again its dryness to fire. And so, in a circle, the matter of earth desires to exist under the form of fire: because fire, as if thirsty, naturally acts upon the earth and converts the matter of earth into its own form. Again, that same matter of earth desires to be under the form of air, which air is, as it were, naturally sensitive to fire. And therefore it acts upon the fire and the matter of earth. And the fire, which had turned the earth into its own form—then that matter naturally desires to be under the form of water. Water, sensing this, acts upon the air and upon that matter which was...

<summary>This page explains the theoretical basis of alchemy using Aristotelian physics, arguing that because the four elements share overlapping qualities (heat, cold, moisture, dryness), they can naturally transform into one another in a cycle.</summary>

Whence **Arnold** <note>original: "Arnoldus" — likely referring to Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist</note> says in his tenth [chapter]: "Most blessed father, **Hermes the philosopher** <note>original: "Hermes philosophus" — Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says that metals consist of the four elements, and each element abounds in its own matter from the four elements, since a simple element is not given to us to act upon." Furthermore, in the matter of metals, it is necessary that the elements have one common matter of bodies, which is common to the form of the elements, so that through it they can be transmuted.

And that same matter which was once water, becomes that of air, earth, and fire. There are, therefore, four qualities or virtues <term>virtutes</term> <note>original: "virtutes" — in this context, it refers to the inherent powers or active properties of the elements</note> proceeding from the existence of the elements, and any of these can be attributed to elemental matter. These virtues are: of heating, of cooling, of dryness, and of moisture. Two of these qualities are active—namely, heat and cold—while two are passive—namely, moisture and dryness. There are, therefore, two elements in comparison to elemental things that are active, namely fire and water, and as it were two passive ones, such as earth and air. To this extent, they are active and passive among themselves, and they communicate in nature.

Hence it is that one element communicates its quality to another, so that by circulating in this way, it can convert the quality of that [other] into itself, and it is transmuted. It should also be known that

It is common to all metals that their matter is very close to one another in nature, in virtue <term>virtute</term> <note>original: "virtute" — referring to the internal power or active property of a substance.</note>, and in potential.

Hence **Albert the Great** <note>original: "Albertus Magnus" (c. 1200–1280) — a Dominican friar and one of the most influential medieval thinkers on nature and alchemy.</note> says: Because in the works of nature he learned by his own sight that "living waters" flow from one origin, and in one part there was gold, and in another silver, yet the matter was one; only the location in relation to heat was different. Therefore, the diversity of the place where the metal was purified produced a diversity according to its species.

For every thing whose root is earth and water becomes subject to death. This is to say, earth becomes water, and the qualities of water overcome it; thus there is the dissolution <term>solutio</term> <note>original: "solutio" — the process of turning a solid into a liquid state.</note> of the body, and the coagulation <term>coagulatio</term> <note>original: "coagulatio" — the thickening or solidifying of a liquid.</note> of the spirit, and vice versa. For they share a single operation: because one is not dissolved unless the other is coagulated. 

Therefore, in the beginning of the work, you should unite the sun <note>Sun represents Gold or the active, masculine principle (Sulfur).</note> through the moon <note>Moon represents Silver or the passive, feminine principle (Mercury).</note>, and coagulate through the sun, for from this the effects will appear, because the lower part is pressed down, since naturally the superior things dominate the inferior.

Hence says **Hali**, king and philosopher <note>original: "Hali rex & philosofhus" — likely referring to Khalid ibn Yazid, an early Umayyad prince and legendary figure in Arabic alchemy known in Latin as Hali Rex.</note>: These both, namely the dissolution of the body and the congealing of the spirit, will occur in one operation, and one does not happen without the other. The reason is, because the body and soul, when they are joined together, each of them acts upon its companion. 

For example, when earth and water are joined together, the water tries to dissolve the earth; with its moisture, its power <term>virtute</term>, and the property that is in it, it makes the earth finer than it was before: and it renders the earth like itself in body, so that it becomes water; and conversely, the water is thickened by the earth and becomes like the earth in density, because earth is denser than water. Therefore, **Albert** says in *The Secret of Secrets* <note>original: "Albertus in Secretis secretorum" — referring to Albert the Great and a popular medieval grimoire/alchemical text attributed to him or Aristotle.</note>:

Then that oil quickly enters inside, and then the Mercury is changed in color, and will be congealed in the form of white glass: extract this vitrified Mercury from the fire. When it has cooled, let one weight [of this] be taken and projected upon sixty weights...

### *How our medicine of the stone cures all diseases and infirmities, and the manner of using it.*

The manner of using the medicine is as follows, according to all the philosophers. If you wish to use our medicine by consuming it, then take of our Elixir the weight of two florin ducats <note>Gold coins commonly used as standard units of weight in the medieval and Renaissance periods.</note> for every one pound of some medicinal mixture <note>original: "confectionis" — a "confection" was a prepared medicinal compound, often involving honey or sugar to make it palatable.</note>, and in winter, eat the weight of one drachm <note>original: "dragmæ" — a small unit of weight, roughly 1/8 of an ounce.</note> of this mixture. And it will preserve health and youth in a man; it makes a young man out of an old one and causes grey hairs to fall out. 

Likewise, our philosophical poison <note>As noted on the previous page, "poison" here refers to the Elixir's potent ability to "kill" or dissolve the existing state of a substance to allow for its transformation.</note> cures leprosy immediately. It dissolves phlegm, purifies the blood, sharpens the sight and all the senses, and sharpens the intellect in a marvelous way beyond all the medicines of the philosophers. Therefore, our medicine is beyond price, since all things were made for the sake of man, etc.

-># ROSARY<-
->### OF THE PHILOSOPHERS ###<-

let him recognize the method <note>original: "regimen". In alchemy, this refers to the specific sequence of heating and governance required to mature the Stone.</note>, which once known, he will not require many things, but only one; nor does it require great expenses, since there is only one stone, one medicine, one vessel, one method, and one arrangement. And you should know that the art is most true. Furthermore, the philosophers would never have studied to express such a diversity of colors and their sequence unless they had seen and touched them. For this reason, we repeat this: all those working outside of nature are deceived and are themselves deceivers. Therefore, let our practice and our focused obedience be within nature, because our stone is of animal, vegetable, and mineral origin <note>This "tripartite" nature refers to the stone possessing the characteristics of all three kingdoms of life: the ability to grow (vegetable), to feel/act (animal), and to endure (mineral).</note>. ### Geber on the Investigation of Truth
<note>original: "Geber de veritatis inuestigatione." Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the "father of chemistry." This text is part of the "Latin Pseudo-Geber" corpus, which was highly influential in medieval and Renaissance Europe.</note>

We have considered in our volumes, based on secret and natural powers and the properties of natural things, and even through our own experience in discovery, a material for investigation that is entirely certain. For we have found nothing else at all, except that those things from which our **medicine** <note>The Elixir or "Stone" used to transform base metals into gold.</note> is drawn for transmuting bodies, must possess within themselves these properties of qualities:

**First:** That it must contain within itself a most subtle and incombustible earth, suitable for fixing—being completely fixed—along with its own proper **radical moisture** <term>radical moisture|radicali humore: the essential, life-sustaining fluid inherent in a substance, believed to be the basis of its existence and stability.</term>.

**Second:** An airy and fiery humidity, uniformly joined, such that if one part is volatile, the other is as well. And this humidity is superior to all other humidities, enduring the heat of the fire until the completion of its sufficient thickening into ash; until its need is met, remaining inseparably annexed to the earth, namely without evaporation.

**Third:** That the natural disposition of the humidity is such that, by virtue of its homogeneity <note>original: "homogeneitatis," meaning the substance is uniform in composition throughout.</note> across all its different properties, it keeps the earth joined to it by a connection between the two. Because in both, through this homogeneity, a virtuous tempering occurs, resulting in a total union and a bond of inseparable connection, equally maintained after the final stage of preparation.

<summary>This page outlines the three essential physical requirements for the alchemical "medicine" as defined by Geber: incombustible earth, stable humidity, and a perfect, inseparable union between the two.</summary>
<keywords>Geber, Investigation of Truth, alchemy, medicine, transmutation, radical moisture, homogeneity, decoction, fixed earth</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the list of properties required for the alchemical "medicine" or Elixir, as described by Geber. It follows the third property mentioned on the previous page, which concerned the homogeneity and natural disposition of the substance's humidity.</meta>

-># ROSARIVM<-

...provide good fusion. **Fourth**, that this homogeneity be of such purity of essence, and artificially cleansed of every combustible or burning thing, so that it does not burn the things it joins at the smallest level <note>original: "per minima" — an alchemical concept referring to the most minute particles or the deepest structural level of matter</note>, but rather protects them from combustion. **Fifth**, that it should possess a clear and splendid **tincture** <term>tincture|tinctura: the transformative coloring power of the Elixir</term> within itself—whether white or red—that is clean, incombustible, stable, and fixed. The fire must be unable to change it, nor should burning sulfurs or sharp, corrosive substances be able to corrupt or ruin it. **Sixth**, that the entire compound, when integrated with its final completion, should be of such subtlety and material tenacity that after the final addition at the end of its cooking <term>decoction|decoctio</term>, it remains in a state of very thin fusion, like water. It must possess deep penetration even to the furthest reaches of the material to be transformed, of whatever kind of fusion its completion consists. Through its closeness and natural affinity, it must adhere to its own vapor <note>original: "fumo" — literally "smoke" or "fume," referring to the volatile spirit of the substance</note> with an inseparable bond. This bond stands firm against the power of fire at its appointed time, spiritually leading the metallic bodies back into its own nature.

Having considered these things, we have found through our investigation seven properties of things that are necessary and timely for our **Stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note>: And these are: **oiliness** <term>oiliness|oleagineitas: a greasy or fatty quality believed to allow the stone to flow and mix with metals</term>, **subtlety of matter**, **affinity**, **radical moisture** <term>radical moisture|radicalis humiditas</term>, **purity**, **clarity**, **fixing earth** <term>fixing earth|terra figens: the solid, stable component that prevents the mixture from evaporating in the heat</term>, and **tincture**.

Indeed, the first property among these differences is **Oiliness** itself, which, during projection <term>projection|proiectio: the final stage of the alchemical work where the Elixir is cast upon base metals to transform them</term>, provides a universal melting and opening of the medicine. For the very first thing necessary after the medicine is projected is its sudden and suitable fusion, which is completed and becomes deeply integrated <note>original: "inuisceratur" — literally "becomes part of the internal organs or viscera"</note> through its natural oiliness.

The second is the **thinness of the matter**, or its spiritual subtlety—thin or flowing upon infusion like water, penetrating into the depths of the substance to be changed. This is because, secondarily after the melting of the medicine, its immediate entry <note>original: "ingressio"</note> is required.

The third is **Affinity** or closeness between the Elixir and the substance to be transmuted, which grants an adherence when it encounters its own kind, as well as retention. This is because, thirdly after the entry of the medicine, a suitable and necessary sticking-together <note>original: "adhærentia"</note> must occur immediately.

The fourth is a **radical and fiery Humidity** <term>radical moisture|humiditas radicalis: the fundamental, life-sustaining moisture believed to exist within all matter, essential for its growth and stability</term>, which congeals and solidifies the parts held together by the adherence of their own kind; it unites all similar parts inseparably and forever. This is because, fourthly after the adherence, the consolidation of the parts is necessary and made possible by its own viscous and essential radical moisture.

The fifth is **Purity and a cleansed clarity**, which gives an eminent splendor when subjected to fire <note>original: "in combustione existenti"</note>, without additions after the consoli-

**Geber** <note>original: "Geber" — referring to Jabir ibn Hayyan, though many of these Latin texts are now attributed to "Pseudo-Geber," a 13th-century European author writing under his name</note>: Note, first, that no **silver** <term>silver|argentum: here referring to the alchemical goal of creating "lunar" or silver-like perfection in metals</term> can be produced unless all things are first dissolved. Second, that no **dissolution** <term>dissolution|solutio: the process of breaking down a solid into a liquid state, the necessary first step in many alchemical operations</term> should be performed except in its own blood or an appropriate blood—that is, in the **water of Mercury**, which is called the **water of the dragon** <note>original: "aqua draconis" — a metaphorical name for a corrosive solvent, likely a mineral acid or a highly purified mercury derivative</note>. Third, that this water of the dragon must be made through an **alembic** <term>alembic|alembicum: a distillation apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube</term> without any other thing being added; and that in the making of it, there is a most great stench. Fourth, that with that water one can dissolve **amalgam**, the **body** and **spirit**, **cinnabar** <term>cinnabar|cinabrium: mercury sulfide, the most common source of mercury in nature</term>, and in short, each and every thing that is of its own nature. Fifth, that the water must be clean; therefore it should not be made except from a purged dragon. The dragon is purged by raising it up <note>original: "eleuando" — likely referring to the process of sublimation</note> three times, and then **vivifying** <note>original: "viuificãdo" — restoring the liquid, "living" state of mercury from a dry or calcined form</note> it. Sixth, that it is necessary for the dissolved material to **putrefy** <term>putrefy|putrefiat: the stage of the "Great Work" where the substance is left to rot or break down, often represented by the color black</term> in heat and moisture—that is, in **horse dung** <note>original: "fimo equino" — horse manure was used as a steady, low-heat source for digestion and fermentation in the lab</note>. From this arises a certain blackness. Seventh, that it should be coagulated in the dry sun of the moisture—that is, in a **water bath** <term>water bath|balneum Mariae: a vessel of hot water used to heat materials gently and steadily, named after the legendary alchemist Mary the Jewess</term>. Eighth, that the time for the perfection of the Elixir is at least one year. However, it is to be seen that it ought to be the time of a human fetus in the mother's womb. Ninth, that **mercury** <term>mercury|mercurius: the fluid principle of all metals</term> is in no way "killed" <note>original: "interficitur" — to 'kill' mercury means to fix its volatile nature so it no longer evaporates when heated</note> except with the scent of a perfect body—red for the red work, and white for the white work; and that the body can give weight while its own weight remains.

There are four things by which our work is com[posed]...

It is necessary that there be more of the volatile than the fixed, from double up to fivefold or sixfold, even up to tenfold and no further. And the more volatile parts there are, the more slowly they are **fixed** <term>fixed|fixantur: the process of making a substance stable and resistant to heat, so it no longer evaporates</term>; the fixed becomes volatile within the space of one month.

And note that it cannot be the Elixir unless the body and spirit pass through all the elements—that is, through the natures of all the elements—so that they first become **earth**, then **air** (that is, vapor), third **water**, and fourth **fire**. This is so that it does not flee from the fire; for **fire** is the name for everything that does not flee fire, and which does not wither or consume in the fire.

Whoever wishes to investigate the secret of this art must know the **First Matter** <term>First Matter|materia prima: the original, primordial substance from which all things are created, sought by alchemists as the starting point of their work</term> of our bodies; otherwise, he will be frustrated in his labor.

The **first matter** <term>first matter|prima materia: the original, undifferentiated substance from which all things are created; in alchemy, the starting material for the Elixir</term> of bodies is not common **mercury** <note>original: "mercurius vulgi" — literally "the mercury of the crowd," referring to ordinary quicksilver as opposed to the "Philosophical Mercury"</note>, but is an unctuous and moist vapor. Because body does not act upon body, nor spirit upon spirit, for the reason that form does not receive an impression from form, nor matter from matter, because like has no **action or passion** <term>action & passion: scholastic terms meaning "the power to act" and "the capacity to be acted upon"</term> upon its like, since neither of them is worthier than the other, because an equal has no command over an equal.

Nothing is made from what is already perfect, because it has already reached its completion. Regarding this principle of nature or artifice, we have an example in bread. Bread that has been leavened and baked is perfect in its state or being and has reached its final end; it cannot be fermented any further. The same is true of gold. Pure gold has been brought through the trial of fire into a firm and **fixed** <term>fixed: in alchemy, a "fixed" substance is stable and does not evaporate or change when exposed to heat</term> body. Among the Philosophers, it is entirely impossible to ferment it further unless one possesses the **First Matter** <term>First Matter: the primordial, undifferentiated substance from which all things are created (materia prima)</term> of metals, in which the gold may be dissolved back into its original state and into its basic, mixable elements. ...it will be gold, and by means of the craft, it is led into the **true ferment of the philosophers** <term>ferment: in alchemy, a substance—much like yeast in baking—that "leavens" or transforms a base metal into a higher state</term>. And let us change this with ingenuity into **perfect matter**, or into the spirit of perfect bodies. For this reason, many among modern workers—even those called Philosophers—are deceived, because they abandon the work at the very point where it should have been started. Woe to you, **sons of doctrine** <note>original: "doctrinæ filij"; a common alchemical term for students or initiates of the "Hermetic" secrets</note>, who hope to gather fruit before it is ripe, and who hope to reap before the harvest.

**Another Philosopher** <note>While unnamed here, this phrase often introduces a citation from ancient authorities like Aristotle or the *Turba Philosophorum*</note> says: From the perfect, nothing can be made, because the species of things that are perfect in their nature are not changed, but rather are corrupted <note>original: "corrumpitur"; in this context, it means the substance breaks down or loses its essential form</note>; nor can anything be made entirely from the imperfect according to the art. The reason is that art cannot introduce the very first foundations (dispositions), but **our stone** <term>our stone: the Philosophers' Stone, the goal of the "Great Work"</term> is a middle thing between perfect and imperfect bodies; and what nature itself has begun, this is led to perfection through the craft. The perfect is not altered, but corrupted. But the imperfect is well-suited to be altered:
->therefore the corruption of one is the<-
->generation of another.<- <note>This is a fundamental alchemical and Aristotelian axiom: *corruptio unius est generatio alterius*. It suggests that for a new, higher substance to be born, the old form must first be broken down.</note>

<summary>This page explains that the alchemist must work with "middle" substances like Mercury, as things already perfect cannot be changed without being destroyed, and things too imperfect lack the necessary foundation.</summary>

## *The arrangement of the vessel suitable for our work, according to the tradition of one called Ferrarius.* <note>Ferrarius, or Efferarius, was an Italian alchemist, likely of the 13th or 14th century, known for his practical instructions on laboratory apparatus.</note>

Let a round glass basin <note>original: "concha vitrea"; literally a glass shell</note> be made, the bottom of which should be small in size, in the manner of a shallow dish. And in its middle, let a collar <term>spondilium: a structural ring or flange used to join parts of a vessel</term> be formed, with a glass band surrounding it. And upon that band, let a round wall be cast, equally distant from the wall of the basin by the thickness of the lid of the basin itself, so that in this space the wall of the lid may fall loosely without pressure.

The height of this wall should be according to the measurement of the height of the basin's wall, or a little more or a little less. Indeed, let two equal lids be formed to the measurement of this cavity between the two walls, whose length should be equal, and let each be two large palms <note>original: "palmarum"; a traditional unit of measurement based on the width of the hand, roughly 7 to 9 inches</note> in size, and let their shape be the same, namely pyramidal.

At the tops of these lids, let there be two equal holes—one in one and the other in the other—into both of which a single hen’s quill could fit. Moreover, the entire purpose of the vessel is that its lid can be removed according to the will of the craftsman, and that the joint be ingenious so that, without any luting <term>lutation: the process of sealing joints in alchemical apparatus with "lutum" (a specialized clay or paste) to prevent vapors from escaping</term>, no exit is open to the spirits—that is, to Mercury and the blue vapor <note>original: "lazur"; referring to "lapis lazuli" or more likely the volatile blue fumes produced during certain chemical reactions</note>. ### On the salt of the philosophers.

The Philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle, the traditional "Philosopher" of the Middle Ages, or an anonymous alchemical authority</note>: Whoever wishes to alter <term>bodies: (original: "corpora") the solid metals</term> and <term>spirits: (original: "spiritus") volatile substances like sulfur or mercury</term>, and change them from their own nature, must first reduce them to the nature of salts and alums; otherwise, he will achieve nothing. The Philosopher: Salts and alums are those things which are produced by our works. Salts are the roots of your work. <note>The legendary founder of alchemy</note> Hermes says: All salts of whatever kind are contrary to our art, except for the salt of our <term>lunaria: (literally "moon-plant") a symbolic name for the substance of the silver-making process</term>. Arnold says: The reason it is not found in [common] salts or alums is this: because [the medicine] must be made; he who seeks from nature what is not in it [seeks in vain]. The Philosopher: The salt of metals allows Mercury to be dissolved into pure water under <note>horse dung, often used as a source of gentle, steady heat for "digesting" substances</note> dung. And that coagulated mixture will be the perfect medicine <note>another term for the Philosopher's Stone or the Elixir</note>.

Note: Every salt well-prepared returns to the nature of <term>sal ammoniac: (original: "salis armoniaci") valued for its ability to sublimate and its role in joining spirits and bodies</term>, and the whole secret lies in prepared common salt. Note: <term>Roman Vitriol: (original: "Vitriolum Romanum") likely copper sulfate</term> has the nature of the stone of metals, and it is hot and dry. Also: <term>Alum</term> seems to be coagulated Mercury, but it falls short of its perfection; it is hot and moist, and it is called the "equal of one," that is, Mercury. Therefore, he who knows the salt and its dissolution knows the hidden secret of the ancients.

### CONJUNCTION

## Arisleus in a Vision <note>original: "Arisleus in visione." Arisleus is a recurring narrator in alchemical literature, specifically the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, who describes the "philosopher's stone" through dream-like allegories.</note>

Therefore, join your son <term>Gabricus: the alchemical "King" or "Sulfur," representing the active, masculine, and solar principle</term>, who is beloved to you among all your sons, with his sister <term>Beya: the alchemical "Queen" or "Mercury," representing the passive, feminine, and lunar principle</term>, who is a radiant, sweet, and tender girl. Gabricus is the male, and Beya is the female, who gives to him everything that is of herself. 

O blessed nature, and blessed is your operation, because from the imperfect you make the perfect. Therefore, do not take up this nature unless it is pure, clean, raw, pleasant, earthy, and upright. If indeed you do otherwise, nothing will be of use. See that you introduce nothing contrary to our <term>stone: the "Philosopher’s Stone," the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting eternal life</term>; instead, set the stone alone. 

Therefore, join our servant to his fragrant sister, and they will beget a son between them who will not resemble his parents. And although Gabricus is dearer to Beya, yet no generation <note>meaning the creation or birth of the new substance</note> occurs without Gabricus. For the sexual union of Gabricus with Beya results in immediate death <note>In alchemy, "death" refers to the "mortification" or "putrefaction" stage where the substances dissolve and lose their original form to be reborn as something new</note>. For Beya climbs upon Gabricus and encloses him in her womb, so that nothing of him can be seen at all. And she embraced Gabricus with such great love that she conceived him entirely into her own nature and divided him into indivisible parts. 

Wherefore <term>Masculinus: likely referring to a specific alchemical authority or a text emphasizing the "masculine" solar principle</term> says:

> *The conception, which had been like milk, changes to blood,*
> *Pale things turn black, and the spread red things become bright,*
> *If the white woman is married to the red husband,*
> *They are soon embraced, and once embraced, they are joined.*
<note>original: "Quæ quasi lac fuerat conceptio sanguinem mutat, / Pallida nigrescunt, rubea diffusa litescunt, / Candida mulier, si rubeo sit nupta marito, / Mox complexantur complexaq; copulantur." These lines describe the color changes—the "Four Stages"—of the alchemical process.</note>

Mark well these words, and note the mysteries, because the spirit which dissolves the **white foliated earth** <term>white foliated earth: a purified, flaky state of the alchemical matter, often called "terra alba foliata"</term> does not allow any of them to remain fixed, unless you have occupied that same spirit with the body from which it was prepared in the beginning. **Permanent water** <term>permanent water: a transformative alchemical solvent that does not evaporate, often identified with philosophical mercury</term>, whether it be called everlasting or **burning wine** <note>original: "vinum ardens," referring to a potent, distilled spirit or alcohol</note>, is called the **water of the body**, that is, when the body has been reduced into **Mercury**. And water is the weight of the wise <note>original: "pondera sapientum," referring to the measure or proportion used by alchemists</note>; therefore, water and fire suffice for you for the whole work. Our water is stronger than fire: because it makes a pure spirit out of the body of gold, which fire cannot do. And fire, in respect to this water, is as water is in respect to common fire. Therefore the philosophers say: Burn our copper <note>original: "æs," which can refer to copper, bronze, or the "base" matter of the work</note> with the strongest fire. **Aristotle**, in the *Regimen of Princes* <note>The "Secretum Secretorum," a popular medieval text falsely attributed to Aristotle, containing occult and political advice</note>, says to Alexander concerning the four elements: When you have water—that is, Mercury—from air—that is, the Sun—and air from fire—namely the spirit of Mercury—and fire—namely Mercury—from earth—namely the Moon—then...

### PHILOSOPHY

...elemental, just as in other elemental bodies. Therefore, the **stone** is called "every thing," because it has within itself and from itself everything necessary for its own perfection. It is found everywhere because of its participation in the elements; it is called by every name because of the worthy and wonderful variety of colors in its nature. It is most vile through **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: the stage of the work where the matter breaks down and turns black, symbolizing death before spiritual rebirth</term> and most precious through its virtue. Among the philosophers, this **mastery** <term>mastery: *magisterium*, the complete alchemical process or the secret method of achieving it</term> is covered and hidden. 

Our **stone** is called "one thing" when the substance of the body and the water are prepared indivisibly, so that one cannot be separated from the other. Our stone is said to be of combustible matter, yet **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius"</note> alone is an incombustible and airy spirit, and therefore it is necessary that it be present in the mastery. 

Likewise, the **stone** that the philosophers seek—in which are the primary elements of minerals, the **tincture** <term>tincture: the spiritual essence or "dye" that transforms base metals into gold</term> and the **calx** <term>calx: the powdery residue left after a substance is heated, representing its purified physical base</term>, the soul and spirit with the body, the fixed and the volatile—is **Mercury**. However, this is not just any common mercury, but that upon which nature has determined its first operations toward a metallic nature and then left imperfect. If you extract this stone from that thing in which it is found, and begin to perform the work upon it toward perfection, starting where nature left off, you will find perfection within it, and you will rejoice.

# THE ROSARY

**Morienes:** <note>Morienes was a legendary 7th-century hermit of Jerusalem, credited with teaching alchemy to the King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> This earth, together with its water, putrefies and is purified; when it has been purified, with the help of God, the whole work will be guided.

# THE ROSE GARDEN
<note>original: ROSARIVM. This refers to the "Rosarium Philosophorum," a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise.</note>

Now the water is thickened with the earth and becomes like dense earth, because earth is thicker than water. Therefore, there is no difference between the dissolution <note>original: "solutionem"</note> of the body and the coagulation of the spirit, nor is there any distinct work in any way, so that one might happen without the other. This is just as there is no separate span of time between water and earth in their union, which might be recognized or separated from one another in their operations. Just as the seed <note>original: "sperma"</note> of the man is not separated from the seed of the woman in the hour of their intercourse: so too is their end-point one, their deed one, and one and the same operation looks upon them both at once.

Therefore Merculinus <note>Merculinus is a pseudonym for an alchemical poet often quoted in medieval texts.</note> says:
> *He calls the mixture of things "intercourse" and "generation,"*
> *The seeds are mixed like milk, which appear mingled together.*

The second stage is **conception**, when the earth is dissolved into a black powder and begins to retain a little of the Mercury <note>original: "Mercurio"; here referring to the "Philosophical Mercury" or the transformative spirit.</note> with itself. For then the male acts upon the female—that is, the **azoth** <term>azoth: the essential transformative agent in alchemy, often symbolized as the "universal solvent" or the beginning and end of all substances</term> acts upon the earth. Therefore Arisleus <note>A legendary figure and narrator in the "Turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note> says: "Males do not beget among themselves, nor do women conceive by themselves. For when males lead females, nature rejoices, and true generation occurs; however, when a nature is joined to an unsuitable foreign nature, it produces no true seed. This is what Merculinus says:
> *Conception changes that which had been like milk into blood.*

The stone is found everywhere because of its true composition: for when those three—the **Sun**, the **Moon**, and **Mercury**—are joined together, the power of the stone exists throughout everything, both in the mountains and in the plains (that is, in the bodies and in Mercury), and in the sea (that is, in dissolved water). # ROSARY

The doctrine states: **Dissolve the bodies and soak up the spirit.** And they use the word "bodies" in the plural because there must be at least two of them <note>The "two bodies" refer to the Sun (gold) and the Moon (silver).</note>. They say "spirit" in the singular, for it is necessary that it be one. There is no **seed** <note>original: *sperma*</note> without the matter of the bodies, except for **Mercury**. And when it is said, "Soak up the spirit," it refers to the operation that **fixes** <note>To "fix" a substance in alchemy is to make a volatile substance (like mercury) stable and resistant to heat.</note> Mercury, and the stone is multiplied. "Multiplied" in this sense means it is repeated.

Also, when Mercury **mortifies** <note>original: *mortificat*; the process of chemically breaking down a substance, often associated with its symbolic "death" or blackening.</note> the matter of the Sun and the Moon, the matter remains like ash. Philosophers call this **Sifting** <note>original: *Cribratio*</note> and **Grinding** <note>original: *contritio*</note>. Regarding this ash, it is said in the *Book of the Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the most influential early Latin alchemical texts.</note> and in the works of Arnold <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a celebrated physician and alchemist.</note>: "Do not despise this ash." 

Furthermore, the aforementioned ash—which belongs to those three—is called by the philosophers the **Unclean Body** <note>original: *Corpus immundum*</note>, because it must be boiled down and **calcined** <note>original: *calcinari*; to reduce a substance to a powder or ash through prolonged heating.</note> until it reaches **whiteness** <note>original: *albedinem*; the *albedo* stage of the work, representing purification and the creation of the White Elixir.</note>. Therefore, Morienes <note>Morienus, a legendary hermit-alchemist credited with bringing alchemical knowledge to the Arabic world.</note> says in the *Book of the Turba*: "Unless you cleanse the unclean body and render it whitened, and unless you place a soul into it, you have achieved nothing in this mastery." 

And so there are two parts: namely, the **calcination** of the stone itself and the **fermentation**. Calcination—that is, the reduction into the form of white ash, or earth, or white lime <note>original: *calcis albę*</note> through the operation of the spirit—is performed by **our fire**, which is the **water of our Mercury**.

Also, when it is said that "the tinged substance tinges," <note>original: *tinctum tingit*; a fundamental alchemical axiom meaning that a substance which has been transformed (stained/colored) now possesses the power to transform other materials.</note> it is understood that if this medicine—having been calcined, dissolved, and coagulated—is fermented toward the white, it becomes **Luna** <note>Silver</note>, with...

...with the sun, it becomes the sun. Likewise, **Geber** <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), an influential figure in early chemistry and alchemy.</note> provides proof regarding the **medicine of the third order** <note>In alchemy, a "medicine of the third order" refers to the highest level of the Elixir or Philosopher's Stone, which has reached its full power to transform metals and heal the body.</note>, and says literally: 

> because for both the white and the red, there is one and the same path with the Sun and Moon, yet they differ in fermentation <note>original: "quia tam ad album & rubeum est vna atque eadem via cũ Sole & Luna, differunt tamen fermentatione."</note>. 

This medicine of the third order is twofold: namely, **Solar** and **Lunar**. Yet it is one in its essence, and there is but one way of acting upon it. However, there is an addition of **yellowness** <note>original: "citrinitas"; a specific stage in the alchemical process—the yellowing—that occurs between the white and red stages.</note> or a yellow color, by which the medicine is perfected from the substance of **fixed sulfur** <note>original: "sulphuris fixi"; sulfur that has been chemically stabilized so that it no longer evaporates when exposed to heat.</note>. This means that both medicines are started with the Sun and Moon. But for the "red" stage, the fermentation is done with the Sun, and for the "white" stage, it is done with the Moon. "Sun" is understood here in two ways: in one way as the **water of the sun**, and in the other as the **body of the sun**, as mentioned above.

Also, when it is said that all colors appear, this is true: because before fermentation—during the processes of **calcination** <note>reduction to powder by heat</note>, **dissolution**, and **fixation**—all colors appear. Likewise, the *Light of Lights* <note>original: "Lumen luminum"; a famous medieval alchemical text often attributed to Aristotle or the Persian scholar Rhazes.</note> says this: 

> And know that they are the same things which whiten and redden from within and without: namely, the Sun, the Moon, and Mercury <note>original: "Et scitote quòd eadem sunt, quæ dealbant & rubificant intrinsecus & ex- trinsecus, scilicet, Sol, Luna, Mercurius."</note>. 

These three, when dissolved and fermented, he calls **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum viuum"; literally "living silver," the common name for mercury.</note>, saying: 

> Quicksilver has in itself body, spirit, and soul <note>original: "Argentum viuum habet in se corpus, spiritum & animam."</note>. 

In the same work, the cause is stated as such:

   Our **sublimation** <note>In alchemy, sublimation refers to heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then collects as a solid again, though here it specifically refers to separating the volatile essence from the solid material.</note> is the raising of the non-fixed parts from the fixed parts. In alchemy, "ashes" represent the solid, non-combustible base that remains after the volatile spirits have been driven off by fire.</note> Wherefore **Morienus** <note>A semi-legendary 7th-century alchemist, often portrayed as a hermit-monk.</note> says: Do not despise the ash, for it is the crown of your heart and the ash of things that endure. Calcination is the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder.</note> Wherefore Morienus says: At the bottom remains the calcined earth, which is of a fiery nature; and thus you have, in the aforementioned proportions, the four elements: I mean **dissolved water**, **whitened earth**, **sublimated air**, and **calcined fire**.

Concerning these four elements, **Aristotle** says in the book *On the Government of Principles* <note>original: "de Regimine principiorum." This refers to the *Secretum Secretorum*, a widely read medieval text falsely attributed to Aristotle.</note>: When you have water from air, and air from fire, and fire from earth, then you will have the full art of philosophy; and this is the end of the first composition, as Morienus says.

**Patience** and **delay** are necessary in our Great Work. <note>original: "magisterio." The *Magisterium* is the technical term for the entire process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> Indeed, haste is from the devil in this work.

**Hermes**: He wishes the dead to be brought to life, and the sick to be healed. The same: It is necessary for you to join **body** and **soul** by grinding <note>original: "contritione." While this usually means spiritual repentance, in alchemy it refers to the physical "wearing down" or pulverizing of materials, often under the heat of the "Sun."</note> in the Sun.

The same: Sow your gold in the **white foliated earth**. <note>This refers to a specific crystalline structure of the purified matter.</note> **Senior** <note>refers to the 10th-century Arab alchemist Senior Zadith (Ibn Umail).</note>: The higher smoke shall descend to the lower, and smoke conceives from smoke. The same: This **divine water** is a king descending from heaven. The same: He is the one who brings back the soul to...

### Vincent on the Stone of the Elixir.

**Vincent** <note>Vincent of Beauvais (c. 1184–1264), a Dominican friar who compiled the "Speculum Maius," a massive medieval encyclopedia.</note> in the *Mirror of Nature*, book one: Within mineral bodies, imitating the operation of nature, the Alchemists have attempted to do in a short time what nature does in a thousand years. This refers to "projection," the final stage where the Stone is thrown upon molten base metal to transform it.</note>. This is called by them the **Elixir**, and it is said to be "the stone that is not a stone": a stone because it is ground, but not a stone because it is melted and flows without evaporating, just like gold; nor is there any other thing to which that property applies. 

**Avicenna** <note>original: "Auicen." ->THE ROSARY<-

...tion. And the **Elixir** is a Greek word <note>original: "verbum graecum." While the text claims a Greek origin, the word is actually derived from the Arabic "al-iksīr."</note> which signifies a "great treasure," or "the best of treasures." And indeed, the Elixir, which mixes itself with the **body** <note>In alchemical texts, "body" (corpus) refers to a solid metal.</note>, is like **tutia** <term>tutia: zinc oxide, a mineral used in the medieval period to color copper yellow, creating brass</term> with copper. But the copper is increased or grows from that tutia; the reason for this is that tutia is an earthly thing, while the Elixir is a spiritual thing, and the nature of its own kind is returned to another kind.

**The Alchemist:** However, the Elixir is made in two ways. In one way, it is made from mineral spirits and prepared clean bodies; in another way, it is made from certain things originating from living beings—namely, from hair, or an egg, or blood, and so forth.

In the first way, it is done thus: Certain spirits are **mortified** <note>original: "mortificantur." In alchemy, "mortification" refers to the process of "killing" a substance—altering its outward form or state to release its inner essence.</note> and **sublimated** <note>original: "sublimantur." Purified by being turned into vapor through heat and then re-solidified.</note> until they become clean. After this, one of the bodies generated by nature is burned until it can be ground; then it is **calcinated** <note>original: "calcinatur." Reduced to a fine powder or ash through intense heat.</note> until it is made clean in the manner of lime.

Finally, the spirits and bodies prepared in this way are ground and **imbibed** <note>original: "imbibuntur." The process of slowly adding liquid to a dry substance until it is completely saturated.</note> with sharp distilled waters. Afterward, they are moistened for so long that they are converted into clear water; then they are congealed; at the last, they are placed in the fire for so long until they are made **fixed** <term>fixed: "fixa." A substance that has become stable in heat and will no longer evaporate or change state.</term>.

### Concerning the manifold fire.

For Fire is manifold, and its quality is diverse, distinguished by certain degrees. For a certain fire in the first degree is hot, and moist in the second—namely, the **heat of a horse’s belly** <term>ventris equi: a traditional alchemical method of providing gentle, steady, moist heat by burying a sealed vessel in a heap of fermenting horse manure.</term>. Its property is that it does not destroy the oil but increases it because of its moisture; for other fires destroy it because of their dryness. Therefore, nothing else in the world is like this except the physical heat of a healthy human body.

The fire of the Sun is indeed hot in the same degree, but it is dry. This [horse's belly fire], however, is that which masters the matter; it is produced from a living thing and is nourished like a child who is given milk in the beginning. For a child is nourished and grows from heat and moisture; so also the fire of the horse increases the oil by its moisture. Moreover, it fixes the **stone** <note>The "Philosopher's Stone" or the evolving substance of the Work.</note> by tempering it with its heat.

### *The fire of junipers.*

An artificial, continuous fire, lasting in the same degree as you wish for one, two, or three months, until the coals are laid bare. Therefore, you must always keep them covered, and you can increase or decrease the heat at your pleasure, and this according to the addition of more or fewer glowing coals. 

In the first place, have sufficient ashes, made only from the wood of the **juniper** <note>Juniper wood was legendary in the Middle Ages and Renaissance for its ability to keep embers alive for a very long time; it was often used as a symbol of endurance or eternal heat.</note>. By placing the ashes inside, the large pot should stand over the heat of a fire so that the ash itself may become warm. And thus, all around the smaller pot, you shall place coals upon the ashes, also made only from the aforementioned juniper wood.

Finally, have still more heated ashes of the same wood, which you shall sprinkle over the aforementioned coals, and you shall cover them very well with their own hot ash. And into that smaller pot...

## General Rules.

Everything is composed of that into which it is dissolved: for ice is converted into water by means of heat; it is therefore necessary that it was water before it was ice. In the same way, all metals were originally quicksilver <term>quicksilver: Latin *argentum vivum*, the common name for mercury</term>, which is evident because when they melt in the fire, they are turned into it. Note here that the philosopher also calls molten metal "Mercury," or quicksilver. Therefore, the reduction of metals into quicksilver in this manner is called this "liquefaction," even though it happens through the violence of fire; nevertheless, because in that intense melting it maintains the appearance of quicksilver, <margin>*</margin>he also names it quicksilver. But this is not the philosophical solution <note>original: *solutio*; the author distinguishes between "layman's" melting (liquefaction by heat) and the "philosophical solution," which is a specialized chemical breakdown of matter</note>, but a "layman's" solution; therefore, it corresponds in some way to the sayings of philosophy regarding what you know in particular.

## *Second Rule.*

Every nature naturally desires to be perfected, and shrinks from and flees destruction: therefore it greedily embrace[s]...

### *Third Rule.*

Everything of a worse nature laboring in any art strives, out of its natural malice <note>original: *malitia*; here meaning a natural tendency toward corruption or resistance to perfection</note>, to destroy the better. And everything of a better nature laboring in any art endeavors to perfect the worse. Therefore, first of all, you must know the natures of things, so that you may know how to discern what is better or worse for a nature, and by what means it is perfected, and by what means it is hindered: and [you must ensure] that the quantity of the worse does not exceed the quantity of the better, otherwise you will err greatly.

### *Fourth Rule.*

Every dry thing naturally desires to drink its own moisture, so that it may be unified in its parts. ->ROSARIUM<-

sulfur is not found on earth, except in so far as it exists in those bodies, the sun <note>original: *sole*; in alchemy, the Sun represents gold</note> and the moon <note>original: *luna*; in alchemy, the Moon represents silver</note>, and indeed in another [body] there is that which is told to no one, unless it is revealed to them by God. For the philosophers have subtly imagined how they might elicit those sulfurs from those more perfect bodies, and purge their qualities through art, so that they might have this in art, through the mediation of nature, which did not appear in them before, although they possessed it fully and secretly earlier. And they by no means allow this to be done without the dissolution of the body and reduction into the first matter, which is quicksilver <term>quicksilver: Latin *argentum viuum*, common mercury, which alchemists believed was the "first matter" or base component of all metals</term>, from which they were made from the beginning, and this without any mixing of foreign things, which foreign natures do not improve our stone: because nothing suits a thing except what is close to it, since it is a medicine of a simple and potent <note>original: *virtualis*; referring to the inherent power or "virtue" of the substance</note> nature, produced from mercurial water, in which gold and silver were first dissolved. For example: if ice is placed in simple water, it is dissolved in it by heat, and returns to the first watery substance, and thus the water is tinged <note>original: *tingitur*; a reference to the "Tincture," the power of the Philosopher's Stone to transform or color other substances</note> by the power, even the hidden one, that was in the ice. But if the ice is not resolved by heat into water, it is not joined to the water, but lies in the water, nor does it tinge that water with its power, which was previously coagulated in it on the part of the species: thus in the same way.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the philosophical nature of gold from the previous page, transitioning from the perfection of its "complexion" to its functional role as the "ferment" of the alchemical work. # R O S A R I V M

They have said that gold <note>original Latin: *aurum*</note> holds itself in bodies just as the Sun does among the stars with its light and splendor. For by it, plants sprout in the earth, and every fruit is perfected by the will of God. Similarly, gold in bodies contains and vivifies every body within itself, because the Elixir is the ferment <term>ferment: a vital catalyst, analogous to yeast in baking, that initiates the transformation and "leavening" of the base metals into the Stone</term>, without which the work is never completed. 

Just as dough without ferment is not leavened nor does it rise, so it is when you whiten, sublime, and purify the bodies, and extract the dregs and impurity from them. Then, wishing to unite, join, and mix them together, apply the ferment to them. Look at how the ferment of dough is nothing other than dough. Meditate, therefore, and contemplate whether the ferment of a thing can be anything other than its own nature. This is the key of all the philosophers. 

And it should be noted that the ferment whitens the composition, inhibits combustion <note>prevents the substance from being destroyed or "burnt" by the fire</note>, and holds the tincture <term>tincture: the potent, penetrating color or spiritual essence that transforms metals</term> so that it does not flee; it softens the bodies and causes them to enter into one another and joins them, which is the goal of the operator. By this science, the bodies are cleansed, and their work is completed, God willing.

Raymond <note>likely referring to the medieval polymath Raymond Lull, to whom many alchemical treatises were attributed</note> in the *Apertorium*: Now through the second part, the stone will color itself; it is fixed and fermented. However, the ferment of the stone for the white work is silver <note>original: *argentum*; associated with the Moon</note>, and for the red work is gold, as the philosophers demonstrate; because without ferment, neither the Sun nor the Moon <note>symbolizing the perfected masculine and feminine principles, or philosophical gold and silver</note> comes forth, nor anything else that exists of its [nature]...

## On the twofold difference of minerals, from the same short treatise.

Mineral bodies are specifically distinguished into two parts: namely, into the metallic part and the mineral part. The metallic part consists of metals that derive their origin from Mercury <note>original: "Mercurio"; the "Philosophical Mercury," considered the primal root of all metallic substances</note>; and the mineral part consists of those that do not derive from Mercury.
Examples of metals: the Sun [Gold], the Moon [Silver], Jupiter <note>original: "Iuppiter"; the alchemical name for Tin</note>, and Mars <note>original: "Mars"; the alchemical name for Iron</note>, and it also includes electrum <note>original: "electrum"; a natural alloy of gold and silver</note>. Examples of minerals: Salts, black vitriols <note>original: "atramenta"; literally "inks," referring to dark mineral sulfates</note>, alums, vitriol, arsenic, and orpiment <note>original: "auripigmentum"; a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note>. ### *That it is impossible for lesser minerals to be made into metals artificially.*

But because it was determined in the preceding chapter that it is impossible for lesser minerals to be made into metals artificially, it remains here to be proved first in this way: because these lesser minerals <note>The Latin text here uses "metalla" (metals), but the context and heading clarify it refers to the "minora mineralia" or lesser minerals</note> are not generated from the first matter of metals, which is Mercury. Their generation differs from the generation of Mercury fundamentally: in form, in nature, and in composition.

Instead, it breaks them down and preserves only those things which are of its own nature. 

For example: if water were mixed with earth, they are separated from one another; because earth seeks the bottom, since it is heavy and dry, while water seeks the surface...

There are also other alchemists <note>original: *Alchimistæ*</note> who labor with the lesser minerals, specifically with the <term>four spirits: in alchemy, these are sulfur, arsenic, orpiment, and sal ammoniac—substances that "fly" from the fire (volatize) rather than remaining stable</term>, such as common sulfur, arsenic, orpiment, and sal ammoniac. For to "tinge" <note>To "tinge" or "dye" in an alchemical sense means to fundamentally change the inner nature of a metal to match the agent of change.</note> is nothing other than transforming the substance being dyed into its own nature during the process, and remaining with it without undergoing any further transformation, teaching nature to battle against nature within the fire. For the nature of the "tinging" agent and the "tinged" substance must be in harmony. 

For example: if you were to tinge lead or tin, or any other such metal, using gold or silver, they would agree in their natures because both sides trace their origin to <term>mercury: the philosophical "Mother" or root of all metallic matter</term>. Thus, the mature is joined to the immature, so that the immature may be perfected alongside it through such a path. 

But since these four spirits are of a different nature than the metals (as has already been sufficiently explained), if they are intended to tinge, I ask: must they convert or be converted? If they are *to be converted* by the metal, then they are not a tincture, as is clear from the definition. If they are *to convert* the metal, then by tinging they would convert it into their own nature, which is earthy and foreign to the metallic nature. For **Geber** <note>the Latinized name of the 8th-century Arabic polymath Jabir ibn Hayyan</note> says in the *Perfect Mastery*: Gold is the most precious of metals. For it is the soul joining the spirit with the body—namely, the imperfect body. For just as the Sun and Moon rule over the other planets, so these two bodies rule over the other bodies of metals, which are converted conformably to the nature of the two aforementioned bodies. And for this reason it is called "ferment," for without it the "seeds" are not improved; and just as a little bit of ferment transforms and raises the whole mass <note>original: *corrumptit... transmutat & eleuat* — "corrupts" here is used in the sense of breaking down the old form to raise it into a new one, like sourdough starter</note>, so it happens in our stone as well. > Son, extract from the ray its shadow: take therefore a fourth part of it—that is, one part of the ferment and three parts of the imperfect body—dissolve the ferment in an equal amount of its own <term>mercury water: likely "quick-silver" or a solvent derived from mercury used to break down the metals</term>; cook them together with a very slow fire, and coagulate that ferment so that it becomes like the imperfect body. Then, with the opening of the vessel closed, in the same way and order as has been described, the preparation is completed in all things.

### *Which are the particulars that are perfected in this art.*

To all observers universally, to whom these present words shall come, I declare that in the entire sequence of the art there are only two <term>particulars: specific chemical processes or "recipes" that lead to a partial result, rather than the "Universal" medicine</term>, which are specifically perfected according to the philosophers and nature: the first particular exists both in the **white** <note>the "albedo" or silver-making stage</note> and in the **red** <note>the "rubedo" or gold-making stage</note>.

And because it contains within itself good, mature, and clean **sulfur**, it is therefore possible for the **Sun** <note>original: "Solem"; Gold</note> and the **Moon** <note>original: "Lunam"; Silver</note> to be made from it specifically.

**The Philosopher:** <note>A general reference to authority, likely Aristotle or a similar sage</note> Let it be mixed through artifice with other metallic bodies, because it is of their same nature, and they themselves were generated from it. Therefore, through artifice, it can be made into them, and it imitates nature’s own **digestion** <term>digestion: a process of slow heating meant to ripen or "mature" a substance, mimicking the earth's natural heat</term> in this regard, so that it may be perfected with them. And thus, it becomes like the metals with which it is joined, without any foreign mixture, since nature simply delights in its own nature <note>original: "natura gaudet suæ naturæ"; a core alchemical principle that "like attracts like"</note> and not in anything foreign. But with the Sun it becomes Sun, with the Moon it becomes Moon, with **Venus** <note>Copper</note> it becomes Venus, and so forth, as each one sends its own power into it. It also contains its own good but immature sulfur, which is matured through the art [of alchemy]. For this reason, other metals—being coagulated and "infected" by **combustible sulfur** <term>combustible sulfur: in alchemy, this refers to the "unclean" or "burning" sulfur that makes base metals prone to corrosion and decay, unlike the "fixed" sulfur of gold</term> specifically—cannot, like Mercury, become the Sun or Moon.

# ROSARIUM

**The first reason:** For if they were transformed into **Mercury** <term>Mercury: in alchemy, this is the "universal spirit" or "water" that forms the base of all metals, not just the liquid metal we know today</term> and mixed with the **Sun** <note>original: "Sole"; refers to Gold</note> and the **Moon** <note>original: "Luna"; refers to Silver</note>, then their Mercury would contain within itself that previously mentioned "bad sulfur."

And if it were purified, it could not be purified to such a degree that it would return to a state of Mercury as it was before such simplicity. Nor could the "body" <note>the metallic substance</note> be dissolved by the Mercury within it; and since it could not be dissolved, it would also be unable to transmit its locked-up power into that body.

Instead, with the natures "iron-locked" <note>original: "feratis"; implying the internal qualities are barred or inaccessible to change</note> on both sides, each would be separated from the other during the **assay** <note>original: "examine"; the trial of a metal's purity, usually by fire</note>. This occurs because the substance does not secretly possess a perfect nature within itself, which would allow them to achieve perfection through their dissolution. It is always necessary for these substances, by means of the "art" <note>the alchemical craft</note>, to be assisted by other perfect bodies—bodies that possess a nature that is already naturally perfect.

**Secondly**, if these substances were joined to perfect bodies while still undissolved, less gold and silver could be produced. This is because, through natural **congelation** <term>congelation: the process of a liquid substance thickening or turning into a solid</term> on both sides, their natures are locked tight. When there is no "medium" <note>an intermediary substance or catalyst</note> to open those natures and allow one power to flow into the other, they cannot be joined by a natural union in a way that allows them to return to the Mercury from which they both originally drew their source. Therefore, by the intensity of the fire, they would be separated from one another through the burning away of the imperfect nature, as is clearly seen. But when...

And these are the labors of the **particular path** <note>The "particular" path in alchemy refers to a specific, limited transmutation of a single metal, as opposed to the "universal" path of the Philosopher's Stone</note>, and in this way gold and silver can be made in a particular manner.

Note that **crude Mercury** <term>crude Mercury: raw quicksilver as found in nature, before any alchemical processing</term> dissolves bodies and reduces them into their first matter or nature; but the "mercury of bodies" <note>mercury extracted from already solid metals</note> cannot do this. This is because of the crudity <note>or "rawness"</note> of its **sulfur**, which it possessed in the "first white earth" from which it was made from clear water at the beginning. Because that crude substance always seeks to corrode what is nearest to its own nature—firstly **gold** <note>original: "aurum"</note>, secondly **silver** <note>original: "argentum"</note>, and so on.

But the other mercury, which has been congealed from bodies, cannot do this; because through **congelation** <term>congelation: the process of a liquid substance thickening or becoming solid</term>, that crude sulfur which was previously in it has been altered in its nature. Therefore, it does not corrode like the first kind, nor does it open what is "iron-locked." Consequently, one power is not transmitted into the other; instead, each remains separate. Thus, they are joined only superficially <note>original: "fluctualiter"; perhaps meaning they are mixed like fluids but not unified</note>, but naturally they remain "iron-locked" on both sides.

Wherefore, through the **assay** <note>original: "examen"; the testing of a metal's purity</note> and the harshness of the fire, the imperfect substance is burned away while the perfect remains. This is because one nature cannot assist the other. But with crude **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento viuo"</note> one can do this: namely, to unlock and open the natures, so that each thing may be near its own nature, having been helped...
