Note that there is a twofold dissolution of bodies: into mercury, by mercury; and into **mercurial water**. The first dissolution is required for <term>particularia</term> <note>The "Particular" path: a limited alchemical process that produces gold or silver from a specific base metal, but does not result in the universal Philosopher's Stone</note>; the second for <term>vniuersalia</term> <note>The "Universal" path: the pursuit of the Philosopher’s Stone, which can transform any substance and heal all diseases</note>. The first dissolution of bodies into Mercury is nothing but a **resolution** <note>original: "resolutio"; a reduction or breaking down of a solid into its liquid or primary form</note>—that is, that through resolution alone, that which was locked <note>original: "seratum"; a common alchemical metaphor for the internal structure of a metal being barred or inaccessible to change</note> is opened on account of the entry of one nature into another; and this resolution belongs to "particular" works. 

The second dissolution is into **mercurial water**, and it happens universally. This occurs not through the mere dissolution of immature sulfur into mercury, but through the **putrefaction** <note>original: "putrefactionem"; in alchemy, this refers to the breakdown and "death" of a substance, which is a necessary precursor to its rebirth in a perfected state</note> of the body and spirit in the moist. For the putrefaction of all natures bound to one another is a dissolution and separation; then the bound parts are separated from one another, and each part from the other. This happens through the separation and dissolution of the elements which are connected in the generation of mercury—namely, water and earth—and these same parts, while they are purged in nature, are joined together through conversion, so that...

Through these things, they can be joined back together by Art just as they were divided; if it were not the case that one quality participated in the nature of another—namely, Water sharing the nature of Earth in coldness, and Air the nature of Water in moisture, and so on—then it would follow that the natural work would be totally destroyed, since the elements would be in their simplest state, just as they were before. Before the generation of mercury, Art would have destroyed nature, beginning from the "head," namely from gold and silver, even back to the beginning, which is **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>.

...[quality], and beyond those principles of simple elements, as they existed before the generation of mercury—to go back that far is impossible in the Art. # THE ROSARY

[the moon contains] in itself white sulfur, just as red gold [does], and yet the essence of fire is hidden within it beneath its whiteness: therefore, it is possible for all silver to become gold. Wherefore the philosopher says:

> There is no gold unless it was first silver.
> <note>original: "Non est aurum nisi prius fuit argentum." This reflects the alchemical belief in a hierarchical progression of metals; silver (the Moon) is seen as a "halfway" point toward the perfection of gold (the Sun).</note>

Thus silver contains in itself some undigested qualities, which can be purged from it by the art; so that it partially passes into **fixed mercury** and into the closest nature of gold. This is because it then contains everything within itself that gold does, through the addition of the **red sulfur of the philosophers**, by which it is further "digested." This causes **yellowing** <note>original: *citrinatio*. In alchemy, this is the transition stage between the white work (Albedo) and the final red work (Rubedo).</note> in it through the joining of the **perfect body** <note>The "perfect body" refers to gold itself or the perfected Stone.</note>, since they are simply of one and the same nature.

However, it is impossible for this to happen in other bodies <note>meaning base metals like lead, tin, or iron</note>, since they do not have such a close proximity to the perfect nature as silver does. Their generation is hindered by combustible and foul-smelling sulfur, nor are they themselves made of mercury [in the same way]. Of this, the philosopher speaks:

> There is no passage from one extreme to another, except through a medium.
> <note>original: "Non fit transitus ab extremo ad extremum, nisi per medium." This is a common Aristotelian principle used in alchemy to argue that base metals must first be brought to a state of silver (the medium) before they can reach the state of gold (the extreme).</note>

That is to say, gold is not generated from mercury unless it has first been silver. Nor do these other metals have within them the sulfur of simple, non-burning fire, but rather a burning <term>sulfur adurens|A "burning" or "combustible" sulfur was thought to be an impurity in base metals that caused them to oxidize or degrade in fire, unlike the "non-burning" sulfur of gold.</term>. Therefore, they cannot be partially transformed into fixed mercury, as was said above by **Aristotle**:

> Let the craftsmen know that they can make things similar to those [precious metals], and tint with red-yellow so that it appears to be gold, and tint white with white until it becomes very similar...
> <note>original: "Sciant artifices..." This is a famous citation from the *Meteora*, often attributed to Aristotle in the Middle Ages, though likely written by Avicenna. It originally argued that alchemists could only imitate the *appearance* of metals, not change their species, though alchemists often quoted it to show what they needed to overcome.</note>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the chemical and spiritual processes required to achieve the "Red Work." Following the previous discussion on "cooking" and acidic solutions, the author here focuses on "subtilization"—the refinement of materials to prevent them from turning into glass (vitrification) and to ensure they can penetrate and transform solid bodies.</meta>

# ROSARY

The reason for its discovery is the **subtilization** <term>subtilization: the process of refining a substance until it is "subtle" or extremely fine, allowing it to penetrate other materials</term> of those things which have neither **fusion** <term>fusion: the ability to melt or flow when heated</term> nor **ingress** <term>ingress: the "entry" or penetration of an alchemical reagent into the pores of a metal to transform it</term>; because of this lack, the great utility of **fixed spirits** <term>fixed spirits: substances that were once volatile but have been made stable and resistant to heat</term> and those things which belong to nature was being lost. For everything that is dissolved must necessarily possess the nature of salt or alum, or something similar to them. Moreover, it is their nature to provide fusion before their **vitrification** <note>original: *vitrificationem*. The process of turning into glass. In alchemy, this was often seen as an "arrested" state where the matter became hard and unchangeable, ending the possibility of further transformation.</note>. Therefore, dissolved spirits will also provide a similar fusion. Since these spirits agree greatly in their nature with bodies and with each other, once fusion is achieved, it is necessary for them to penetrate the bodies through that fusion—to penetrate by transforming, and to transform by penetrating.

To this point, however, one does not arrive without the **magistery** <term>magistery: from the Latin *magisterium*, referring to the secret, expert technique or the "masterwork" of the alchemist</term>. This consists in the following: after the dissolution and **coagulation** <note>original: *coagulationem*. The process of thickening or solidifying a liquid.</note> of the substance, some purified but **non-fixed spirit** <note>original: *spiritibus purificatus non fixus*. A volatile substance that has been cleaned but not yet made heat-resistant.</note> should be administered to it. It must be **sublimated** <term>sublimated: heated until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, a process used for purification</term> by that spirit as many times as necessary until the spirit remains with it, granting it a faster fusion and preserving it from vitrification during that fusion.

*For it is the nature of spirits and bodies not to be vitrified, and to save that which is mixed with them from vitrification, so long as the spirits remain within it. Therefore, the spirit which better preserves its nature defends more against vitrification; however, a spirit that is only purified preserves it more effectively than one that is purified, fixed, calcined, and dissolved. For this reason, it is necessary to mix it in; for from these things results a good fusion, an entry, and a stable fixation.* From the work—

### PHILOSOPHY

...principles of nature, therefore, we can prove that only those substances which preserve the nature of salts, alums, and similar things are soluble. For in examining all of nature's works, we do not find any others to be dissolved except those. Therefore, whatever is to be dissolved must necessarily be dissolved by means of their nature, through the repetition of **calcination** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in a crucible until it is reduced to a fine, dry powder</term> and **solution** <term>solution: the process of dissolving a solid substance into a liquid medium</term>. Because of this, we prove that all calcined materials approach the nature of salts or alums; therefore, they must necessarily share those same properties.

The method of solution is twofold: namely, by **warm dung** <term>warm dung: known in Latin as *fimum calidum*, this was a standard alchemical method for providing a gentle, constant heat (roughly 100°F) via the natural fermentation of a manure pile</term>, and by boiling water. These share the same intention and produce the same effect. 

The method using dung is as follows: the calcined material is placed into a **glass flask** <term>ampulla vitrea</term>, and over it is poured a quantity of **distilled vinegar** <term>acetum distillatum</term> (or a similar substance) in an amount double that of the material. The neck of the flask is then blocked so it cannot "breathe" <note>original: *ne respiret*. This indicates an airtight seal, preventing any vapors or "spirits" from escaping during the process.</note>, and it is left under warm dung for three days. Afterward, the dissolved portion is removed by means of **filtration** <note>original: *distillationem philtri*. In early chemistry, this specifically referred to "distillation by the filter," where liquid is drawn through a cloth or felt wick into a separate container to clarify it.</note>. The portion that remains undissolved must be calcined again, and after that calcination, it is dissolved again in the same manner, until the entire substance is dissolved through the repetition of the work.

The method which is done through the boiling of water is faster. It is performed by arranging the calcined material in a flask in the same way with vinegar, with the opening blocked so it does not breathe. This flask is then "buried" in a **cauldron** <term>caldarium: a large pot or boiler used here as a water bath</term> filled with water and straw <note>The straw acted as a cushion to prevent the glass flask from cracking against the hot metal of the cauldron.</note>, just as we have previously instructed in the order for the method of distillation by water. And afterward, the fire is kindled... <note>The page ends with the catchword *accen*, short for *accende* or "kindle."</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of metallic composition and the alchemical "Sulfur-Mercury theory." While the previous page focused on the practical operations of the magistery (fusion and coagulation), this section provides the theoretical foundation for why these processes work, citing Aristotle’s Meteorology as a primary authority on how metals form within the earth.</meta>

### PHILOSOPHY

The nature of all meltable things <term>meltable things: Latin *liquefactibilium*, referring to metals that can be liquefied by heat</term> comes from quicksilver <note>original: *argento vivo*. Quicksilver, or mercury, was considered the "mother" or the watery principle of all metals.</note>, out of its own substance, because it is the property of quicksilver to be coagulated by the vapor or heat of white or red sulfur that is "non-burning." Hence **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE). His work *Meteorology* was the standard source for medieval theories on the formation of minerals and weather phenomena.</note> says in the fourth book of his *Meteorology*:

If the sulfur is white and non-burning, it congeals mercury into good silver; but if the sulfur is a little clear-red, and in it there is the power of a "fiery-ness" that is simply non-burning, it congeals the mercury into the purest gold—better even than what the mine <note>original: *minera*. Refers to the natural ore produced by the earth.</note> has produced. This happens because every dry thing naturally drinks up its own moisture, so that it may be held together in its parts.

Therefore, the vapor of the quicksilver’s sulfur must be coagulated from an earthy substance that is subtle, airy, cooked, and "undigested" <note>original: *indigesta*. In alchemy, "digestion" refers to a slow, steady heat that matures a substance; "undigested" suggests matter that hasn't yet reached its final, perfected state.</note> from the first mixture united to itself by the action of heat. Afterward, it is elevated, cooked, and digested until it possesses the sulfurous power of coagulating quicksilver into metallic bodies.

**Gold** has much of the power <note>original: *virtute*. Here meaning the active quality or essence.</note> of sulfur and little of its physical substance, but it has much of the substance of mercury and little of its power. For this reason, by account of the mercury, it is extremely heavy; and by account of the sulfurous power, it is very red. **Silver**, however, behaves in a completely opposite way: it has much of the substance of sulfur but little of its power, and little of the substance of mercury but much of its power. Therefore, silver is white, because color follows—

# ROSARY

...a multitude of virtue <term>virtue: from the Latin *virtus*, meaning inherent power or medicinal potency</term>, but the virtue is located in the vapor. Its matter is closer to the matter of gold than any other metal; therefore, it is easily turned into gold. It requires no other labor except for changing the color and providing weight.

->*The difference between oil and water regarding the nature of the tincture.*<-

->Arnoldus<- <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous Catalan physician and alchemist. Many influential medieval alchemical texts were attributed to him.</note>

There is a difference between the tincture <term>tincture: a substance used to "stain" or transform the color and properties of a base metal into gold or silver</term> of water and of oil, because water only washes and cleanses, but oil stains and colors. An example of this is: if a cloth is submerged in water, it is cleansed by it, and when it is dried, the water recedes, and the cloth remains in its original state and in its color, just as it was before, except that it is cleaner.

It is the opposite with oil: for if a cloth is dipped in it, it is not separated from it by the heat of fire or air, unless the whole thing is destroyed. Nor can the oil be separated from the cloth itself, except through washing and the drying power of fire. Water, however, is the spirit <term>spirit: the volatile, watery principle that acts as a solvent or carrier</term>, extracting this soul <term>soul: the fixed, essential principle (often the color) that gives a substance its identity</term> from the bodies. But when the soul is extracted from the bodies themselves, it remains carried in the spirit itself, just as the dye of dyers is carried by water onto a cloth. Afterward, the water recedes through drying, and the tincture remains fixed in the cloth because of its oiliness <term>oiliness: Latin *oleoginositas*, referring to the unctuous, non-volatile quality that allows the alchemical "soul" to penetrate and permanently bond with the metal</term>.

<summary>This page explains why oil is a better metaphor for the alchemical tincture than water, arguing that while water only cleanses, oil permanently stains and penetrates "bodies." It describes the "spirit" (water) as a carrier that extracts the "soul" (color/oil) to fix it onto a substance.</summary>

Thus, therefore, the water is the spirit <term>spirit: the volatile, watery principle that acts as a solvent or carrier</term>, in which is carried the tincture of the air <note>original: "tinctura aeris." This refers to the subtle, transformative essence often associated with the color or "soul" extracted from the air or a vaporous state.</note>. When this water is brought back upon the white foliated earth <term>white foliated earth: a purified, crystalline state of the alchemical matter that has been processed until it appears in thin, leaf-like layers</term>, the spiritual water is immediately dried, and the soul—which is the tincture of the air—remains in the body. Therefore, the spirit retains the soul just as the soul retains the body, because the soul does not remain in the body except through the mediation of the spirit. But when they **are truly joined**, they may never be separated, because the spirit retains the soul just as the soul retains the earth. 

For this reason, Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy.</note> commands that souls be venerated in stones, for their dwelling place is within them. Furthermore, these stones are retentive of "fugitives" <note>original: "fugitivorum." In alchemy, "fugitives" are volatile substances, like mercury, that easily evaporate or escape when heated.</note> when joined with them. Therefore, this is our coagulation <term>coagulation: the process of turning a liquid or volatile substance into a solid state</term>, because they hold back that which is fleeing. Sow the soul, therefore, into the white foliated earth, because the earth itself retains it. For when it shall have ascended from the earth into heaven, and shall have descended again into the earth, it will receive the power of the things below and the things above <note>This is a direct reference to the "Emerald Tablet," a foundational alchemical text which describes the circulation of energy between the celestial and terrestrial realms.</note>, etc.

### *On the method of sublimating and whitening, and a recapitulation of the entire mastery.* <term>mastery: also known as the Magisterium, the complete process of creating the Philosopher’s Stone</term>

When the earth has absorbed from the water a fiftieth part of itself, quickly sublimate <term>sublimate: to heat a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again in a purer form</term> it with the strongest fire you can manage, until the substances rise upward in the manner of a very white powder.

When you see the earth as white as snow, like a "dead" powder, adhering to the Aludel <term>Aludel: a series of pear-shaped ceramic pots used as condensers in the sublimation process</term> and its joints, and to the sides of the vessel, then repeat the sublimation upon it without the dregs remaining at the bottom. This is because a "fixed" <term>fixed: a substance that is stable and does not evaporate or change when heated</term> part of it remains attached; if it were allowed to stay with the dregs, it would become permanently bonded to them, and could never be separated from them by any kind of human ingenuity.

The powder that rises upward from the dregs is "ash from ash" <note>This phrase implies a refined essence extracted from a burnt material.</note> and earth that has been extracted, sublimated, and honored. That which remains below, however, is the "ash of ashes"—the lower ash which is reviled, condemned, mere dross and slag. Therefore, distinguish between that which is clear and its limpid part; for when the substance has ascended as white as snow, the work will be complete. Collect it carefully so that it does not vanish into smoke, for this itself is the "sought-after good." It is the white foliated earth <term>white foliated earth: a symbolic term for the purified matter at the Albedo stage, often described as having a flaky or leaf-like structure</term>, which congeals that which is to be congealed, and purifies arsenic and white sulfur. The multiplication of the Elixir is achieved in two ways: one is through the repeated dissolution and coagulation of the Stone; the second is through the <term>projection</term> <note>original: *proiectionem*; the process of casting a small amount of the concentrated Elixir onto a larger mass of base metal to transform the whole into medicine</note> of the first Stone of the Elixir upon a body, either white <note>silver</note> or red <note>gold</note>, in such a quantity that the body itself is also converted into medicine. # ROSARIUM

### PHILOSOPHY

if you do this twice. The same Arnold <note>Arnold of Villanova, a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> says in another chapter: If, however, it melts with more difficulty, which is due to a lack of <term>inceration</term> <note>original: *cerationis*; the process of softening a substance to a wax-like state</note>, assist it with oil—that is, the element of air—by dropping it drop by drop over a light fire until it melts like wax. This is because when you "wax" the material, you are mixing in more of a hot and moist nature than a cold and dry one; and when you <term>fix</term> <note>original: *figis*; making a substance stable so it no longer evaporates</note> it, you are mixing in more of a cold and dry nature than a hot and moist one. Therefore, understand what I say: the perfection of this work is the transformation of nature itself. From the things said above, note that water, air, and oil are the same thing—namely, the <term>spirit of mineral mercury</term> <note>original: *spiritus mercurij mineralis*; the volatile, animating essence extracted from metallic ores</note>, etc.

The same author says in another chapter: The modes of the <term>regimen</term> <note>original: *regiminis*; the controlled sequence of alchemical operations</note> that convert into one another are four principal stages: namely, dissolving, washing, reducing, and fixing. To <term>dissolve</term> <note>original: *soluere*</note> is to turn the coarse into the simple and to refine it; to <term>wash</term> <note>original: *abluere*</note> is to turn the dark into the light; to <term>reduce</term> <note>original: *reducere*</note> is to turn the moist into the dry; and to <term>fix</term> <note>original: *figere*</note> is to stabilize the volatile upon a fixed body.

To dissolve is to divide the bodies and to create the "matter" or the <term>primary nature</term> <note>original: *naturā primam*; the "First Matter" (materia prima), the chaotic base state of all things</note>. To wash is to perform <term>inhumation</term> <note>original: *inhumare*; literally "burying" the vessel in warm dung or earth to maintain a steady temperature</note>, to distill, and to <term>calcine</term> <note>original: *calcinare*; heating a substance to a high temperature to reduce it to powder</note>. To reduce is to "fatten" the material, to wax it, to impregnate it, and to refine it. To fix is to perform the "marriage," to resolve, and to coagulate.

->Through the first, nature is changed internally:<-
->through the second, externally:<-
->through the third, superiorly:<-
->through the fourth, inferiorly.<-
